reviews.first_10_seconds: "AI's electricity, water and CO2". Okay, so it's about whether ChatGPT is bad for the planet? There's a quiz, so I'll tap one. I don't know what a Wh is, but the buttons are big and orange, so I'll guess. I use ChatGPT for homework, so I do want to know whether that's "bad".
reviews.verdict: The guessing card got me. I tapped Boiling a kettle, it said "Not quite", and that felt like a game. After that it turned into a school textbook from America. All the comparisons are a US home, a US EPA phone charge, France, Virginia, Dominion and PJM. I've never heard of most of them, and nothing is about India, my phone, my house or rupees. The answer text uses "0.34 Wh" and "485 TWh" as if I know what those are, and I don't. The page never tells me in normal words. The reveal also doesn't clearly show which button was right. And the "right" answer, "a few seconds of a phone charge", isn't even correct by the site's own numbers: 0.34 of 19 Wh is about 2% of a charge, which is around a minute or two of charging, not a few seconds. The Today page asked me the same question I'd just answered on the home page, so I wouldn't come back tomorrow. I wouldn't send this to friends yet. Nothing in it is funny or surprising enough to put on WhatsApp, and there's no line I could send that says "bro, did you know…". If the first card gave me one shocking, easy comparison about my own life, I'd play all 11.

issues.where: Front-door guess card, right answer 'A few seconds of a phone charge' (reviewed.py line 57)
issues.problem: This is arithmetically wrong. The page's own figures are 0.34 Wh per question and about 19 Wh per phone charge (US EPA), so one question is about 1.8% of a charge. With a normal 10 to 20 W charger that is roughly 1 to 4 minutes of charging, not 'a few seconds'. The option is also unsourced, because no checked quote gives charging time.
issues.fix: Change the option to something the numbers support, e.g. 'About 1/50th of a phone charge' or 'Less than 2% of a phone charge', and show the sum in the reveal (19 Wh ÷ 0.34 Wh ≈ 56 questions per charge). If you keep a time-based option, source a charger wattage first and show the division.

issues.where: Reveal after a guess
issues.problem: The reveal says 'Not quite. Less than a phone charge.' but never says which option was right. The correct button only gets a thin white outline, which I didn't notice; my wrong pick stays bright orange and looks like the winner. 'Less than a phone charge' also doesn't tell me how much less.
issues.fix: Mark the correct option clearly (green or 'Right answer' label) and fade the wrong pick. Start the reveal with the punchline in numbers I can feel: 'About 56 ChatGPT questions = one phone charge.'

issues.where: Everywhere: the card reveal, range bar, bigger picture and ladder
issues.problem: Wh, kWh and TWh are never explained. For a teen who has never thought about electricity, '0.34 Wh' and '485 TWh' mean nothing, and the reveal leads with them. The range-bar caption 'Wh per short text question: from 0.24 (Google (Gemini))…' has nested brackets and reads like a lab report.
issues.fix: Lead every reveal with an everyday comparison and put the unit second. Add a one-time tap-to-explain on 'Wh' ('a watt-hour: a 1-watt LED on for an hour'). Write 'Google Gemini' without the nested brackets.

issues.where: 'Bigger picture' line, ladder fold and bills topic
issues.problem: Every comparison is Western: France, a US home for a day, US EPA, Virginia, Maryland, Dominion, PJM. Reviewed answers mention India zero times. An Indian visitor gets nothing about their own country, their home's use or rupees, and 'more than France' doesn't land. The bills topic is a list of US utility questions.
issues.fix: Add one India-relevant rung or comparison from a sourced dataset (e.g. India's yearly electricity demand from the same Ember dataset next to the 485 TWh, or a typical Indian home's daily use if a checked source exists). Let the topic page say 'Mostly about the US so far', so non-US visitors know why.

issues.where: Today page (Hum #142)
issues.problem: Today's question is the same 'One short ChatGPT question…' card as the front door, so I've already answered it. It feels like a fake daily feature and gives me no reason to return. It also shows no score or result line I could send to friends.
issues.fix: Make Today a different card from the home card, or rotate the home card so it never shows Today's question. After the guess, show a copyable share line like 'Hum #142: I guessed wrong ⚡ humearth.org/today'.

issues.where: Answer page range bar (Google-search myth)
issues.problem: The bar is on a log scale with no label, so 0.34 looks close to 0.24 and 2.9 looks close to 1.86. The caption ends in a broken fragment: '…middle 0.34 (OpenAI). the 2.9 Wh behind "10×".' (lowercase, no verb). The tiny 9px monospace labels are hard to read on a phone.
issues.fix: Use a linear scale, or write 'log scale' under the bar. Rewrite the caption as a full sentence: 'The dotted line is the old 2.9 Wh figure behind the "10×" claim.' Raise label size to at least 12px.

issues.where: Answer page verdict row: 'PARTLY' plus 'OUT OF DATE' chip
issues.problem: Two stamps side by side confuse me. Is Hum's answer out of date, or the claim? I read it as 'this page is old, ignore it'.
issues.fix: Rename the chip to 'Claim uses old numbers', or put it on the claim line ('The claim (from 2024, using a 2009 figure)') instead of next to Hum's verdict.

issues.where: Draft answer pages (e.g. 'Will data centres keep pushing bills up')
issues.problem: The drafts are dense jargon: 'PJM auction cleared at the price cap', '6,600 MW short of PJM's reliability target', 'consumer advocate'. A teenager stops reading after one line. Search sends people into 299 of these, so most search results will feel like this.
issues.fix: In search results, rank the 11 reviewed answers first, and show the bold one-line summary as the result snippet. On draft pages, collapse the long paragraph under 'More detail' so the bold sentence stands alone.

keep: Guess first, then reveal. It's the only part that felt like a game and made me read on. Keep it as the first thing on the home page.
The one-line promise plus the 'Heard something? Ask Hum.' search box with the 'is AI raising my bill?' example. I understood straight away that I can ask things.
The big, thumb-sized orange answer buttons and the 'Just tell me' escape link.
The 'How big is that?' ladder, where each rung says how many times bigger it is than the one above. That's the most understandable thing on the answer page.
Verdict stamps (YES / PARTLY / NO) on topic lists and the bigger-picture list. I can scan for the answer without reading.
The clear 'Draft' label and the dashed draft box. It's honest without being scary.
Quotes 'checked on the page' with a date. Even as a teen I can see this isn't made up.
reviews.persona: a 15-year-old in India who only uses a phone and has never thought about electricity

reviews.first_10_seconds: Right, so it's a site that answers "is AI bad for the planet" questions with sources. Then there's a quiz. I tap "boiling a kettle" because that's what I'd guess, and it says "not quite, less than a phone charge". So asking ChatGPT is basically nothing? Then why does the next box say all the data centres use more than France? I still don't know whether I should feel bad about it.
reviews.verdict: The guessing card got me. It's the only reason I stayed past the first screen, and I'd send the ChatGPT-versus-phone-charge one to my sister, who keeps telling me off for using it. But I came with one question: is my using AI bad, and should I stop? After two minutes I have two facts that seem to argue with each other. One question is tiny, but the total is bigger than France. Nothing joins them up into "here's what that means for you". Below the card it's American. The bills topic is PJM, Dominion and Virginia. The ladder ends at "a US home for a day", and the phone figure is from the US EPA. I'm in Leeds, so the one thing that might matter to me, my bill, has nothing for me. The answer pages are honest and careful, and I trust them more than a newspaper. But they're written for someone who already knows what "Wh", "PJM" or "IEA's 2024 report" mean. The tiny grey range-bar labels are unreadable on my phone. I'd share the card. I wouldn't come back, because nothing says what's new or what applies to me.

issues.where: Front-door card, right answer 'A few seconds of a phone charge' (reviewed.py line 57)
issues.problem: The arithmetic doesn't support 'a few seconds'. 0.34 Wh is about 1.8% of the 19 Wh EPA phone charge. That's roughly 1 minute on a 20 W fast charger and 2 to 4 minutes on a normal 5 to 10 W charger, not seconds. The card that everything else rests on understates the figure by about 10 to 50 times in time terms. Any sceptic who does the sum will throw the whole site out.
issues.fix: Express it as a share of the charge, which needs no assumption about charging time. Make the right option 'About 1/50th of a phone charge' (19 ÷ 0.34 ≈ 56). Or, if you keep a time framing, state the charger wattage and source it, e.g. 'about a minute on a fast charger'. Put the sum in calc[].

issues.where: Reveal headline after a wrong guess ('Not quite. Less than a phone charge.')
issues.problem: The headline doesn't say which option was right, or by how much. 'Less than a phone charge' was also true of 'a few seconds', so it reads as hedging. I also had to read a Wh number to work out the answer.
issues.fix: Make it 'Not quite: about 1/50th of a phone charge. A kettle is about 300 times more.' Highlight the correct button in the same colour as the ticked verdict. Name the scale jump in household terms before any Wh appears.

issues.where: Reveal → 'The bigger picture' line, and every answer page
issues.problem: It gives 'your question is tiny' and 'the total is bigger than France' with no 'so what'. That's the exact confusion a parent arrives with, and it's left unresolved, so the visitor leaves without the answer they came for. ('Should I feel guilty / stop?')
issues.fix: Add one plain 'What this means for you' sentence under the reveal, sourced like everything else. Something like: 'Your own chats are a rounding error next to your car or heating. The growth comes from everyone's use added up, plus video and agents. The choices that matter are made by companies and governments.' Then link to the agents/video and big-tech answers.

issues.where: Topic page 'Your bills and the grid', ladder 'A US home for a day', 'US EPA' phone figure, search placeholder 'is AI raising my bill?'
issues.problem: For a UK visitor, the placeholder invites the bill question, then delivers PJM, Dominion, Virginia, Maryland and Ohio drafts. The ladder's top household rung is a US home (28 kWh), about three times a UK home's daily use. It feels like a site for Americans.
issues.fix: Either add one reviewed UK/Europe bills answer (e.g. Ofgem/NESO on data-centre demand, Ireland's share) at the top of the bills shelf, or label US answers 'US' in the row. Add a UK-home rung next to the US one, sourced (e.g. Ofgem typical consumption). Make the placeholder region-neutral until there's a UK answer.

issues.where: 'The bigger picture' world clause: '485 TWh in 2025, more than France (481 TWh)'
issues.problem: It claims 'more than France' on a 4 TWh (under 1%) gap. The comparison is an IEA estimate against Ember measured demand, and the IEA figure has a wide uncertainty band. Hum's own rule is to show ranges, so stating a strict 'more than' breaks it.
issues.fix: Say 'about as much as France uses (481 TWh)'. Or show the IEA's low/high band next to France's figure, and only say 'more than' if the low end clears 481.

issues.where: Home, the section heading 'The bigger picture' below the card, and the 'Coal, at about 30%' row
issues.problem: The same label, 'The bigger picture', is used for the world-total clause and for a list of questions, which is confusing. In that list, the power-mix row puts 'Coal, at about 30%' in the verdict column where YES/PARTLY sits. It looks broken and reads as if coal is the verdict.
issues.fix: Rename the list to 'Other questions people ask'. For non-yes/no answers, show a neutral 'ANSWER' stamp and move 'Coal, about 30%' into the grey subline.

issues.where: Answer page range bar and caption (Google myth)
issues.problem: The bar labels (0.24, 1.86, 'the 2.9 Wh behind "10×"') are about 8px monospace and unreadable on a phone. The caption ends in a lowercase sentence fragment: 'middle 0.34 (OpenAI). the 2.9 Wh behind "10×".'
issues.fix: Set bar labels to at least 12px. Turn the caption fragment into a sentence: 'The dotted line is the old 2.9 Wh figure the 10× came from.'

issues.where: Answer page stamps 'PARTLY' + 'OUT OF DATE', ladder 'about 1× the rung above'
issues.problem: Two stamps side by side make me ask whether it's partly true or just out of date. The body's conclusion is 'roughly similar, not proven', so neither stamp says it. 'About 1× the rung above' (99 vs 90 Wh) reads as a bug.
issues.fix: Use one stamp with a short reason ('PARTLY · based on old figures'). In the ladder, write 'about the same as the rung above' when the ratio rounds to 1.

issues.where: Today page
issues.problem: 'Hum #142' shows the identical card to the home page's first card. On a return visit it looks like nothing changes, which kills the reason to come back.
issues.fix: Make Today pick a different card from the home default, and add a line saying what tomorrow's topic is.

keep: The guess-then-reveal card on the front door. It's the one thing that made me engage instead of bouncing.
The one-line promise 'AI's electricity, water and CO2: straight answers, every number sourced.' It's clear in a few seconds.
Plain-English claim → verdict → answer structure on answer pages; 'Why the claim misleads' is the bit I'd actually quote to someone
Sources quoted word for word, with 'checked on the page' and the date, plus 'COMPANY SAYS SO' labels. They make it feel more trustworthy than a news article.
The 'What nobody knows yet' fold. Admitting gaps builds trust.
The 'How big is that?' ladder in everyday things (phone, kettle, home), once the rungs make sense for a UK reader
The clear dashed 'Draft' box on unreviewed answers
No sign-up, no tracking
reviews.persona: a busy UK parent who heard AI is bad for the planet and has two minutes

reviews.first_10_seconds: Something about AI and electricity, and it wants me to play a guessing game about ChatGPT, which I don't use. "Is AI raising my bill?" in the search box is the only line on that screen about my life. I can hear the fans from my garden in Loudoun every night, and my Dominion bill keeps going up. The first thing they show me is a phone-charge quiz. I'd type "bill" into the box, and if that didn't answer me fast, I'd close it.
reviews.verdict: I stayed past a minute only because the search box offered "is AI raising my bill?". After that the site let me down where it matters to me. The reviewed bills page gives me "PARTLY", PJM auction revenue in billions and a note that there's "no checked figure for the effect on an average household bill per month". Two taps away, the site's own drafts have exactly what I came for: the Virginia regulator's roughly $13.60 a month base-rate increase, a state study forecasting $14 to $37 a month extra by 2040, and a page about the hum near data centres. So the polished part of the site is the part that doesn't answer me, and the useful part is stamped "Draft" and filed in a list. The home page is built for someone curious about their chatbot, not for someone living next to the buildings. I'd forward the Loudoun property-tax and noise drafts to my HOA, because those are fair and specific. I wouldn't come back to play a daily phone-charge quiz. The first card's right answer also looks wrong to me: 0.34 Wh is about 2% of a 19 Wh phone charge, which is a minute or two of charging, not "a few seconds". If the first number I see is off, why trust the rest?

issues.where: Home and Today first card, the correct option 'A few seconds of a phone charge' (reviewed.py line 57)
issues.problem: 0.34 Wh divided by the site's own 19 Wh phone charge is about 1.8% of a full charge. At ordinary 5 to 15 W charging that is roughly 1.5 to 4 minutes, and even a 30 W fast charger takes about 40 seconds. 'A few seconds' understates it by 10 to 50 times. It's the headline answer on the very first card, and the site's own ladder ('about 56x the rung above') contradicts it.
issues.fix: Change the option to 'About a minute or two of phone charging' or 'About 1/50th of a phone charge'. Make the reveal show the arithmetic: 0.34 Wh / 19 Wh ≈ 2%.

issues.where: Reviewed answer 'Are data centres making my electricity bill go up?' (slug bills): 'What nobody knows yet'
issues.problem: It says there is no checked figure for the effect on an average monthly household bill. The site's own drafts cite the Virginia SCC approving about $13.60 a month in base-rate increases (2026 to 2027) and a Virginia state study forecasting $14 to $37 a month extra by 2040. One page says the number doesn't exist while another prints it. Readers will think the site is hiding the figure or is sloppy.
issues.fix: Promote the SCC and JLARC figures into the reviewed bills answer, after checking their quotes on the page. Say which part is attributed to data centres and which isn't. Rewrite the 'nobody knows' line to something narrower and true, for example 'nobody has measured how much of a given bill increase is caused by data centres'.

issues.where: Reviewed bills answer, plain answer and stamp
issues.problem: For someone in Virginia the answer is abstract: 13 states, the 'independent market monitor', '$7.3 billion (82%)' of auction revenue, 'about 9% of the wholesale power price'. None of it says dollars on my bill. 'PARTLY' reads as a dodge when the monitor calls data centres the primary reason in PJM, which is where I live.
issues.fix: Open with a dollar line for PJM and Virginia residents, for example 'If you're on Dominion: base rates up about $13.60 a month by 2027; a state study forecasts $14 to $37 more by 2040; data centres are the main driver of PJM's capacity price jump, by the monitor's estimate.' Keep PARTLY only for the global claim, and add 'Yes, in PJM' as the regional sub-verdict.

issues.where: Home page: first card and section lists
issues.problem: The front door assumes the visitor is an AI user wondering about their own footprint. Neighbours (bills, noise, diesel generators, water, taxes, how close they can build) are the people most likely to be angry and searching. Their questions don't appear on the home page at all. 'Near you' is only a topic shelf further down.
issues.fix: Add a second door next to the card, such as 'Live near a data centre?', linking to the bills, noise (q320), generators (q322), setback distance (q327), Loudoun taxes (q343) and Virginia share (q295) pages. Or rotate the first card so a bills or neighbour question leads half the time.

issues.where: Drafts in 'Your bills and the grid' and 'Near you' (Dominion q143, noise q320, generators q322, Loudoun taxes q343, Virginia share q295)
issues.problem: These are the most valuable pages for my county, and they're fair and specific. They're labelled 'Draft' with a dashed 'may change' box, so I'm told not to trust them, while a reviewed page about video clips gets the polish.
issues.fix: Choose the next batch of pages to review by audience anger, not by AI-footprint curiosity. Review the Dominion bill, noise, generator, setback and Loudoun tax pages before more chatbot comparisons.

issues.where: Range bar labels and caption, ladder notes, small grey text throughout (template.html .range text 12 to 13px mono; grey sub-lines)
issues.problem: On a phone the range-bar numbers ('0.24', '1.86', 'the 2.9 Wh behind "10x"') are tiny monospace, grey on near-black. I can't read them without glasses. The caption 'middle 0.34 (OpenAI). the 2.9 Wh behind "10x".' is a broken sentence fragment with a lowercase 'the'.
issues.fix: Use at least 14px for every label on the bar and 16px for the caption, and raise the grey contrast to WCAG AA or better. Rewrite the caption as a full sentence: 'The dotted line marks the old 2.9 Wh figure behind the "10x" claim.'

issues.where: Home page: 'The bigger picture' used for both the reveal callout and the section heading below; the answer page's 'The bigger picture' next-link
issues.problem: The same label means three different things: a world-total sentence, a list of questions, and a link. In the list, the right-hand column mixes a verdict stamp ('YES') with a result ('Coal, at about 30%') in mono caps, which reads like an error.
issues.fix: Keep 'The bigger picture' for the world-total callout only. Rename the home list 'Questions people ask', and show only a verdict stamp or a short result, styled the same way.

issues.where: Answer page ladder: 'about 1x the rung above' (Boiling 1 litre of water)
issues.problem: 'About 1x' is meaningless filler, and 90 Wh to 99 Wh looks like the same bar length.
issues.fix: Hide the multiplier when it's under 1.5x, or say 'about the same as the rung above'. Consider dropping the video-clip rung so the kettle sits right after the phone charge.

keep: The search box with 'is AI raising my bill?' as its example: it's the one line on the home screen that speaks to me
The 'Your bills and the grid' topic page: 24 questions, reviewed answers first, Dominion and PJM questions by name
The draft pages on noise, generators, setback distance and Loudoun property tax: specific, balanced, and they name company claims as claims
Verbatim source quotes with 'checked on the page' and dates, and the 'COMPANY SAYS SO' label
The 'What nobody knows yet' fold. Admitting gaps earns trust, as long as it doesn't contradict the site's own drafts
'These are the monitor's estimates, not measured bills': plain honesty about what a number is
The Google-search myth page: it shows where the 10x came from (a 2009 figure) instead of just saying 'wrong'
No sign-up, no tracking
reviews.persona: a retiree in Loudoun County, Virginia, who can hear a data centre from the garden and is angry about bills

reviews.first_10_seconds: A fact-check desk for AI energy claims: type in the thing you heard, or play a guessing game, and get a sourced number. The headline promise is clear enough. What I actually want is one citable figure with a date and a source, and the front door gives me a quiz instead.
reviews.verdict: The sourcing work underneath is the real thing, and it's rarer than it should be. Verbatim quotes are dated "checked on the page", company figures are labelled "Company says so", the calculations are shown, and the gaps are named ("OpenAI hasn't published how its 0.34 Wh is measured"). I'd bookmark that as a reporter. But the top layer, the part I'd paste into copy, breaks the rules the bottom layer keeps. The first card's correct answer, "a few seconds of a phone charge", is wrong by Hum's own sums: 0.34 Wh is about 1/56 of a 19 Wh charge, which is minutes of charging, not seconds. That card is the first thing every visitor sees. The headline comparison "485 TWh, more than France (481 TWh)" puts an IEA modelled estimate next to Ember's demand figure and calls a 0.8% gap "more than". An editor would strike that. The range bar puts Google, OpenAI and an MIT-measured open model on one axis even though they draw different measurement boundaries. That breaks Hum's own no-ranking rule, and the axis is log scale with no label on the reveal. There's also no "cite this" line. I'd use Hum as a research trail, but I wouldn't share it until the headline numbers are as careful as the footnotes.

issues.where: Front-door card and Today card (q002 guess, right=0 'A few seconds of a phone charge') in reviewed.py
issues.problem: Arithmetic error in the correct answer. By the page's own figures, 0.34 Wh ÷ 19 Wh is about 1.8% of a phone charge, roughly 1 to 2 minutes on a typical 1 to 2 hour charge, or about 30 seconds even on fast charging. 'A few seconds' understates it by an order of magnitude, on the most-seen screen of the site. The reveal headline 'Not quite. Less than a phone charge.' then doesn't match the option that was marked correct.
issues.fix: Change the option to one you can derive from the cited figures, e.g. 'About 1/50th of a phone charge', or 'A minute or two of charging' with the charge-time assumption shown in calc. Make the reveal headline restate the right option with its sum ('About 1/56 of a phone charge: 0.34 Wh vs 19 Wh').

issues.where: WORLD line ('more than France (481 TWh)'), on every reveal and answer page
issues.problem: 485 TWh is an IEA modelled estimate of data-centre consumption, and its uncertainty is far wider than 1%. 481 TWh is Ember's 'electricity demand' for France, which is defined differently. Calling a 0.8% gap 'more than' is false precision, and the consumption-vs-demand basis is never stated. CLAUDE.md requires saying consumption vs generation explicitly. A journalist who repeats this gets corrected.
issues.fix: Say 'about as much as France uses in a year (IEA estimate, 485 TWh; France about 481 TWh, Ember)'. Name the basis of each figure ('consumption' / 'demand'). Or pick a comparator with a clear margin.

issues.where: Range bar on q002 and the Google-myth page (low 0.24 Google Gemini, mid 0.34 OpenAI, high 1.86 MIT TR open model)
issues.problem: Three figures with different, partly unpublished measurement boundaries sit on one axis, each labelled with a company or model name. Readers will treat that as a ranking of models, which breaks Hum's fixed rule. The answer text adds to it by turning the endpoints into '10 to 80 questions per charge'. The page also admits that OpenAI's boundary is unknown.
issues.fix: Label the bar 'published figures, measured differently, not comparable model to model'. Drop the model names from the endpoint labels on the bar (keep them in sources). Add a one-line boundary note per figure in the sources fold (e.g. Google: includes idle and cooling; MIT TR: GPU energy doubled as an estimate; OpenAI: not stated).

issues.where: Range bar (template.html line ~176), reveal and answer pages
issues.problem: The bar is log scale, but only the ladder fold says so. On the Google-myth page the 2.9 Wh marker sits just right of 1.86, so 2.9 looks barely bigger than the top of today's range. The caption also ends in a lowercase fragment: 'middle 0.34 (OpenAI). the 2.9 Wh behind "10×".'
issues.fix: Print 'log scale' under every range bar, or switch to a linear scale for ranges that span under 20× (0.24 to 2.9 fits fine). Fix the caption to 'The dotted line is the 2.9 Wh behind the "10×" claim.'

issues.where: Answer pages, the 'Send this answer' / Copy to share box
issues.problem: There is no citation line, and that's what I came for. Copy-to-share gives social text, but no 'Cite: figure, primary source, publication date, Hum page URL, checked date'. I'd have to rebuild the citation from the sources fold, and I may cite Hum instead of the IEA by mistake.
issues.fix: Add a 'Cite this number' button that copies one line, e.g. '0.34 Wh per short ChatGPT query (OpenAI, Sam Altman blog, June 2025; boundary not disclosed). Via humearth.org/…, checked 18 Oct 2026.' Name the primary source first.

issues.where: Draft pages (e.g. 'Is Dominion raising Virginia bills because of data centres?')
issues.problem: The verdicts don't answer the question asked. The draft says bills rise '$13.60 a month' from a base-rate case, but nothing cited ties that rise to data centres. The gaps admit the SCC order and the JLARC report were never read, and the figures come only from Cardinal News and Annandale Today. Yet the banner says 'Each quote below was checked on its page', which a reader takes as a primary check. Search surfaces 299 of these, so they far outnumber the 11 reviewed pages.
issues.fix: When a draft rests only on press reports, change the banner to say 'checked against news reports, not the original document'. Rank reviewed answers above drafts in search. Hide drafts whose verdict sentence doesn't address the causal claim in the question.

issues.where: 'How big is that?' ladder
issues.problem: 'Boiling 1 litre of water, 99 Wh, about 1× the rung above' (99/90 = 1.1). A rung that's 1× wastes a step and reads like a bug. The kettle figure is also Hum's own physics sum, mixed in among sourced rungs, and is flagged only in the small print.
issues.fix: Drop the AI video or the kettle rung, or show the ratio to one decimal ('1.1×'). Tag the kettle rung inline with 'Hum's calculation' in the same style as the 'Company says so' label.

issues.where: Today page and 'The bigger picture' list
issues.problem: Today #142 is the same card as the home page, so returning visitors get nothing new. In the verdict column, 'Coal, at about 30%' appears in the same monospace style as YES/PARTLY verdict stamps, which muddles what a verdict is. The 'OUT OF DATE' stamp next to PARTLY doesn't say whether the claim or Hum's answer is out of date.
issues.fix: Make Today differ from the home card. Show only verdict values in the stamp column (use a plain result line for the coal answer). Rename the stamp 'Claim uses old data'.

keep: Verbatim source quotes with 'Quote checked on the page, [date]', a check that most AI-energy coverage never does
'Company says so' vs 'Estimated' vs 'Measured' labels on each source
'What nobody knows yet' fold, especially naming that OpenAI hasn't disclosed what its 0.34 Wh includes and that Google hasn't published a current search figure
Shown calculations (e.g. 0.34 Wh × 473 g/kWh ≈ 0.16 g; 246 kg ÷ 0.16 g ≈ 1.5 million), which I can check in seconds
The Google-search myth page: it traces the 10× to the IEA's 2.9 Wh and Google's 2009 figure, and lands on 'roughly similar, not proven' instead of a cleaner false verdict
Netflix and flight answers that state their boundary mismatch (streaming includes your device, questions don't)
Clear Draft labelling and the gaps lists on drafts
Plain search box with 'Heard something? Ask Hum.' as the entry point
reviews.persona: a climate journalist on deadline who needs one citable number and checks everything

reviews.first_10_seconds: It's a site that answers the "AI is boiling the oceans" claims my Year 10s bring in from TikTok, with a quiz card on top. The quiz card is the bit I'd put on the board as a starter. I get that much in ten seconds. What I can't see is anything telling me what a "Wh" is, or how I'd run it in a lesson.
reviews.verdict: I want to use this. The guess-then-reveal card is a ready-made starter activity. The myth pages, with a verdict, the claim quoted, "Why the claim misleads" and real sources, are exactly the source-evaluation lesson I struggle to resource. But I can't put it in front of 30 teenagers tomorrow. The very first card marks a factually wrong option as correct. At OpenAI's 0.34 Wh against the EPA's 19 Wh phone charge, one question is about 1/56 of a charge, which is a minute or two of charging, not "a few seconds". A sharp kid with a calculator will catch that, and I lose the room's trust in the whole site. The water page says the bottle-per-email claim was a retelling of the UC Riverside range, yet the page itself admits it couldn't read the article where the bottle-per-email figure actually comes from. The big-tech page stamps YES on "because of AI" while saying neither company separates out AI. Nothing explains Wh, kWh or TWh, and that is the first hand that goes up. Fix those, add a one-screen unit explainer, and I would use it and send it to my department. For now I'd show the Netflix and flight pages myself, not hand out the link.

issues.where: Front-door card / Today card (reviewed.py q002 guess, right=0 'A few seconds of a phone charge')
issues.problem: The marked-correct answer is arithmetically wrong. 0.34 Wh ÷ 19 Wh is 1.8% of a charge. A phone takes about 1.5 to 2 hours to fill, so that is roughly 1 to 2 minutes of charging, not seconds. Even the lowest figure (0.24 Wh) is over a minute. The reveal then says 'Not quite. Less than a phone charge.', which doesn't match any option and is vaguer than the answer the student picked against. This is the very first thing every visitor sees.
issues.fix: Change the correct option to 'About a minute of phone charging' or 'About 1/50 of a phone charge', and add the sum to calc: '19 Wh ÷ 0.34 Wh ≈ 56 questions per charge'. Make the reveal headline restate the right option ('Right: about a minute of charging. A full charge is ~56 questions.'). Add a build check that every guess option with a number or duration has a calc line.

issues.where: Answer page 'bottle-of-water' (q003): verdict NO, the answer text and 'Why the claim misleads'
issues.problem: The page asserts the claim came from 'a bottle per 10 to 50 answers' being retold as a bottle per answer. The widely shared 'bottle per email' figure actually comes from a 2024 newspaper analysis with the same UC Riverside researchers, about a 100-word GPT-4 email. The page's own 'What nobody knows yet' admits that source exists and wasn't read. So the origin story and the flat NO are unverified, and possibly wrong. Students who Google it will find that article in one click.
issues.fix: Until the newspaper figure is checked on the page, stamp it PARTLY or NOBODY KNOWS. Rewrite 'why' as: 'One researcher estimate for GPT-4 in a hot, water-hungry location came to about a bottle per email; company figures for today's models are about 1,000 times lower; nobody independent has measured current models.' Drop the 'retold' story unless it is sourced.

issues.where: Answer page 'big-tech-emissions' (q023) stamp YES, and the home 'bigger picture' list
issues.problem: The question is 'going up because of AI?' and the stamp says YES. The page's own unknowns say neither company separates AI from other data-centre work, and the sources are trade-press summaries, not the reports. A YES on a causal claim the evidence can't isolate teaches students exactly the overclaiming the site exists to correct.
issues.fix: Use PARTLY with the result 'Yes, because of data centres; how much is AI isn't published.' Keep the 18% / 37% / 25% figures. Keep the 'company figures' chip and add a 'via trade press' chip.

issues.where: Everywhere a unit appears: card reveal, range bar caption, ladder, bigger-picture box
issues.problem: Wh, kWh and TWh are never explained. '0.34 Wh', '28 kWh' and '485 TWh' sit next to each other with no bridge. A 14-year-old cannot read the headline comparison, and I'd spend the lesson explaining units instead of the argument. The ladder exists but is folded away and also mixes Wh and kWh.
issues.fix: Add a permanent one-line key under the first reveal and at the top of the ladder: 'Wh = watt-hour, the energy a 1-watt light uses in an hour. 1 kWh = 1,000 Wh. 1 TWh = 1 billion kWh.' Make each unit a tappable term showing that line. Show the ladder rung values in a single unit column (Wh, with kWh/TWh in brackets).

issues.where: Range bar on reveal and answer pages (google-search: 0.24–1.86 with the 2.9 marker)
issues.problem: The bar is a log scale with no label on the card. The ladder says so, the bar doesn't. Visually 0.34 sits right next to 0.24, and the 2.9 claim marker sits just past 1.86, so the bar understates the gap students are supposed to see. The 8px mono tick labels are unreadable on a classroom projector. The caption also has a broken sentence: '...middle 0.34 (OpenAI). the 2.9 Wh behind "10×".'
issues.fix: Use a linear scale for ranges that span less than 20×, or print 'log scale' on the bar itself. Raise tick labels to at least 12px. Fix the caption: 'The dotted line is the 2.9 Wh figure behind "10×".'

issues.where: World-total clause (WORLD in reviewed.py), repeated on almost every page
issues.problem: '485 TWh ... more than France (481 TWh)' presents a 4 TWh (under 1%) gap between an IEA estimate and a measured national figure as a ranking. The IEA estimate's uncertainty is far wider than 4 TWh. A student who checks the next IEA revision could find it flips. It's also the same sentence on every page, so it reads as boilerplate.
issues.fix: Say 'about as much as all of France uses (481 TWh)'. Vary the clause per page so it connects to that page's question (the water page already does this well).

issues.where: Search results and topic shelves mixing 11 reviewed answers with 299 'Draft' answers
issues.problem: I can't let students search freely. 96% of what they'll land on is labelled 'Not reviewed yet: the wording and verdict may change'. Drafts are listed with a DRAFT tag in the verdict column, but there's no way to restrict them. The bills shelf is almost entirely US (PJM, Dominion, Virginia), which means nothing to a class outside the US.
issues.fix: Add a 'Reviewed only' toggle that defaults on, remembered per browser (no account needed). Show the count ('11 reviewed, 299 drafts'). Label shelves that are US-only ('US: PJM region') so non-US teachers know to skip them.

issues.where: Today page ('Hum #142') and the whole site's dark-only theme
issues.problem: '#142' implies 141 past questions that don't exist, and the Today card is identical to the home card, so a returning student sees nothing new. The single dark theme washes out on most classroom projectors, and there's no print view for a worksheet.
issues.fix: Start the numbering at #1, or drop it until there is a real archive. Rotate the Today card from PLAY by date so it differs from the home card. Add a print stylesheet (light, sources expanded, one answer per page) as the classroom handout; it costs no tracking or accounts.

keep: The guess-first card: four concrete options, then a reveal with a range. It's a ready-made lesson starter, and the 'Just tell me' escape is good.
The claim pages' structure: the claim quoted in full, a verdict stamp, 'Why the claim misleads', 'What nobody knows yet'. That is a media-literacy lesson in one page.
Sources with the verbatim quote, a 'Quote checked on the page' date and a COMPANY SAYS SO / ESTIMATED label. This is what makes it citable in a student essay.
The 'How big is that?' ladder from one question to a US home to all data centres, with 'about 56× the rung above'. It's the best scale-building device on the site.
The Netflix and flight pages: they show their arithmetic (77 ÷ 0.34 ≈ 230; 246 kg ÷ 0.16 g ≈ 1.5 million) and admit the boundaries differ. Students can redo the sums themselves.
The honest 'Draft' labelling and the 'Prototype for testing' banner. Keep that candour even after the fixes.
No sign-up, no tracking. I can use it in a school without a data-protection form.
reviews.persona: a secondary-school teacher deciding whether to use this in tomorrow's lesson

reviews.first_10_seconds: OK, it's a fact-check site for "AI is boiling the oceans" takes. I can type in something I've heard or play a guessing card, and I get a number with a source. That's what I'd hope for. But the headline puts "AI's electricity, water and CO2" next to a world total that covers every data centre. I'll stay, but I'm watching for the guilt trip.
reviews.verdict: This is the first "AI energy" site I'd send to the person in a group chat who keeps posting the water-bottle line. It says NO to the bottle, NO to the flight and NO to Netflix, shows its working, and puts the quotes where I can check them. That earns real trust. Two things nearly lose me. First, the very first card is wrong. Its right answer is "a few seconds of a phone charge", but 0.34 Wh is about 1.8% of a 19 Wh charge, which is one to two minutes on a normal charger. The headline card being wrong is the one mistake a sceptic like me will screenshot. Second, every card ends with the same "bigger picture": all data centres, more than France, doubling by 2030. That figure is all data centres, not AI, and the gap to France is under 1%. After telling me my question costs almost nothing, the page slips the guilt back in with a scarier number about something else. The site also contradicts itself on thinking modes (10 to 100 times more on one page, 150 to 700 times on another). And the range bar ranks Gemini against OpenAI against Llama, which breaks your own rule about comparing across different measurement boundaries. Fix those four and I'd share it without hedging. Right now I'd share the bottle and flight pages and skip the home card.

issues.where: Home and Today guess card, one-question (reviewed.json guess.right = 0, 'A few seconds of a phone charge')
issues.problem: The arithmetic is wrong. 0.34 Wh ÷ 19 Wh is about 1.8% of a phone charge. A full charge takes 1 to 2 hours, so 1.8% is about 1 to 2 minutes, not 'a few seconds'. Even a fast charger gives about 30 seconds. At the 1.86 Wh high end it is about 10% of a charge, roughly 6 to 12 minutes. The reveal headline 'Less than a phone charge' then dodges the option you marked right. This is the first thing every visitor sees.
issues.fix: Change the right option to 'About a minute of charging a phone' (or '1/50th of a phone charge'). Make the reveal line 'Right: about 1/50th of a phone charge (0.34 ÷ 19 Wh)' and put that sum in calc[]. Add a build check that recomputes each guess option from the sourced figures.

issues.where: The 'bigger picture' line on almost every reveal and answer page, and the home headline
issues.problem: The headline says 'AI's electricity…', but the world figure (485 TWh) covers all data centres: streaming, banking, this website. It is attached to a card that has just shown one question is tiny, and to the 0.2 kg-a-year page. That is the AI-shaming move: a reassuring per-use figure, then a scary total for something wider. It also breaks the CLAUDE.md rule to say what is being counted.
issues.fix: Say 'All data centres (AI is one part of this)' and add the sourced AI-share figure from constants.source.json next to it. On per-use pages, make the bigger picture the AI share or the 'my year' figure rather than the France line every time.

issues.where: World line, '485 TWh in 2025, more than France (481 TWh)'
issues.problem: The site claims 'more than' on a 4 TWh (0.8%) gap. It compares the IEA's modelled data-centre consumption with Ember's demand figure for France, which is a different measurement, and the IEA estimate itself has a wide range. That is false precision on the most-quoted sentence on the site.
issues.fix: Write 'about as much as France uses in a year' and drop the ranking word. Keep the two figures in the sources fold.

issues.where: one-question answer vs reasoning answer
issues.problem: The figures conflict. one-question says 'a thinking mode can use 10 to 100 times more', built from Epoch's long-input figures of 2.5 and 40 Wh (which are about long context, not thinking). reasoning says 30 times on average and 150 to 700 times for the same model. A sceptic will spot this and stop trusting the rest.
issues.fix: In one-question, split it into 'a long pasted document: about 7 to 120 times (Epoch AI)' and 'a thinking mode: see the reasoning page, measured on open models at about 30 times on average'. Link it with next.deeper. Add a cross-page consistency test for multipliers.

issues.where: Range bar on one-question and google-search (lowNote 'Google (Gemini)', midNote 'OpenAI', highNote 'large open model')
issues.problem: Placing Google's median Gemini prompt, OpenAI's undisclosed average query and MIT TR's doubled-GPU estimate for Llama 405B on one axis makes Gemini look cheapest and open models look worst. That ranks models across different measurement boundaries, which Hum's own rules forbid. Calling all three 'per short text question' also papers over median vs average vs one test prompt.
issues.fix: Label the bar 'published figures (each measured differently)' and drop the low/mid/high model names from the axis. List each figure with its boundary (median, average, GPU×2) in the caption. Or show the range without naming companies at the ends.

issues.where: flight answer: 'AI video and all-day coding agents use far more per task'
issues.problem: For heavy users like me it hand-waves exactly the question we care about. The drafts already contain a sourced coding-agent answer (about 41 Wh per median Claude Code session, about 1,300 Wh a workday, from developers' own token logs).
issues.fix: Promote 'How much electricity does a coding agent use?' to the reviewed set. Link it from flight and my-year with the real figure: about 1.3 kWh a workday ≈ 0.6 kg CO2, still far below a flight. Label it 'a user's own estimate, no company figure'.

issues.where: Range bar caption on google-search (template.html line 189)
issues.problem: The claim note is pasted on as a broken fragment: 'middle 0.34 (OpenAI). the 2.9 Wh behind “10×”.' The bar is also on a log scale with no label, so 2.9 appears to sit next to 1.86.
issues.fix: Render it as 'The dotted line is the 2.9 Wh behind “10×”.' Add 'log scale' under the axis, as the ladder already does.

issues.where: Ladder rung text and the power-mix stamp slot
issues.problem: 'about 1× the rung above' (video clip vs kettle) reads like a bug. On the home list, 'Coal, at about 30%' sits in the YES/PARTLY verdict column in the same stamp style, which muddies what a verdict is. The Today page repeats the home card exactly, with 'A day of a fridge' already highlighted.
issues.fix: Show 'about the same as the rung above' when the ratio is under 1.5. Style non-claim results as plain text, not stamps. Make Today a different card from the home card and clear its focus state.

keep: Verdicts that say NO to the water bottle, the flight and Netflix, with the arithmetic shown. This is the reason someone like me would share it.
Verbatim source quotes with 'checked on the page' and company figures labelled 'Company says so'
'What nobody knows yet' fold: admitting OpenAI hasn't published its boundary is more convincing than any number
The google-search page explaining where the 10x came from (a 2009 Google figure against the IEA's 2.9 Wh) instead of just calling it wrong
Guess-first card mechanic and the 'Heard something? Ask Hum.' search: the purpose is clear in 10 seconds
The 'How big is that?' log ladder from one question up to a home's day
my-year answer (about 0.2 kg a year against 4.7 t per person): the most useful number on the site for ending an argument
Clear 'Draft' labelling on the 299 unreviewed answers
reviews.persona: a software engineer who uses AI all day and is tired of "AI shaming"

reviews.first_10_seconds: It's a myth-buster for AI's electricity, water and CO2. The first thing it asks me to do is guess how small my ChatGPT question is, and the answer comes from Sam Altman's blog. So far it reads like "relax, your AI use is tiny." The real story, a France-sized and doubling total, is in a quote box under the card, not at the front door.
reviews.verdict: The sourcing is real and better than most climate sites. Quotes are checked on the page, company figures carry a "Company says so" tag, and the arithmetic in the reviewed answers holds up (0.16 g per question, 1.5 million questions per flight, 0.22 kg a year, 10 to 80 questions per charge). The editorial choices are the problem. Most of the reviewed, playable cards are about one person's use, and each one reassures me: a question costs "a few seconds of a phone charge", the water bottle is a NO, Netflix is a NO, flying is a NO, Google search is "roughly similar", and my year is 0.2 kg. That is the per-query frame the industry wants, and the anchor for it is OpenAI's unexplained 0.34 Wh, sitting in the middle of every bar and in every share text. The answers that hold companies to account are all buried. Meta's location-based emissions are 43,000 times its market-based figure. "100% renewable" is really 65% hour by hour. Training and the chips themselves are left out. All of these sit in unreviewed drafts. Of the 11 reviewed answers, only big tech's emissions is about companies, and it ends by repeating their net-zero pledges. The first card's correct option is also off by a big factor, in the reassuring direction. As it stands I wouldn't send this to anyone in my network. People would share the "NO" cards to tell climate people to calm down. Fix the framing and the front door and I'd use it every week.

issues.where: Front door and Today card one-question (reviewed.json q002, guess.right = 0: 'A few seconds of a phone charge')
issues.problem: The arithmetic is wrong, and the error flatters the industry. At 0.34 Wh against Hum's own 19 Wh phone charge, one question is about 1/56 of a charge. A normal 1.5 to 2 hour charge makes that about 1.5 to 2 minutes of charging, or roughly 30 to 60 seconds even on a fast charger. 'A few seconds' understates it by about 10 to 40 times. This is the first answer every visitor sees, and the reveal ('Less than a phone charge') never backs up the option it marks as correct.
issues.fix: Change the right option to 'About 1/50 of a phone charge' or 'A minute or two of charging your phone'. Show the sum in calc: 19 Wh ÷ 0.34 Wh ≈ 56. Add a build check that recomputes every guess option from the sourced numbers.

issues.where: Front door: choice of the first playable card and the order of PLAY in template.html line 163
issues.problem: The first impression is 'your question is tiny', anchored on Altman's blog figure, which the page itself says has no published method. Six of the 11 playable cards reassure about personal use. The systemic cards (power mix, emissions rising, bills) come later in the rotation or below the fold. That is exactly the 'individual footprint' frame the companies promote, and it lets them off the hook.
issues.fix: Open with a systemic card, for example 'Which source supplies the most electricity to data centres? Coal, about 30%' or 'Data centres used as much as France in 2025 and will double by 2030'. Alternate personal and systemic cards in PLAY, and never put two reassuring 'NO' cards in a row.

issues.where: Range bars on one-question and google-search (low = Google Gemini, mid = OpenAI, high = MIT TR large open model)
issues.problem: One bar places three figures measured on different boundaries. Google's figure is a comprehensive median, OpenAI's method is unknown, and MIT's is a GPU-based estimate on Llama. That breaks Hum's rule against ranking models across measurement boundaries. It also makes an unverified company number the visual 'middle', the single figure the page treats as the answer.
issues.fix: Present the range as 'published figures from 0.24 to 1.86 Wh' with no mid marker, or mark the 0.34 as 'OpenAI's claim, method unpublished' in the company-claim style. Label each end with its boundary ('chips only' vs 'whole data centre'). Use 'one company's claim' wording in the headline answer, not 'about 0.34 Wh'.

issues.where: Reviewed set: the 11 answers versus drafts.json
issues.problem: The answers that hold companies accountable are drafts only. Meta's location-based emissions (5.86 Mt) against its market-based figure (135 t), a 43,000-fold gap. Google's '100% renewable' really meaning about 65% carbon-free hour by hour. Llama's 'zero emissions'. Training costs and embodied chip emissions. Meanwhile 4 of 11 reviewed answers debunk worries about personal use.
issues.fix: Before testing, promote and review at least three company-claim answers: the Meta market vs location gap, the meaning of 100% renewable, and training plus chips. Put one of them in the playable rotation. Rewrite the 100% renewable draft's soft verdict ('Both are true') so it says plainly that the 100% is a paper total and the grid reality is about 65%.

issues.where: Big tech emissions answer (q023), final sentence
issues.problem: The answer ends by repeating Google's net-zero and Microsoft's carbon-negative 2030 pledges, unchallenged, while their emissions rose 18% and 25%. That gives the companies the last word. Separately, the scope 2 quote saying emissions fell 3% is market-based, and the page doesn't explain that.
issues.fix: End on the gap instead: 'Both still pledge net zero or carbon negative by 2030, with emissions now moving the other way.' Add a 'What nobody knows yet' line on how the pledges rely on certificates and offsets, linked to the market vs location answer. Label the 3% figure as market-based.

issues.where: Flight answer (q107) and the my-year answer (q004)
issues.problem: Both compare one question with one flight or with one person's footprint, and the 'Why the claim misleads' text says the real comparison is the total. Then the total is never given in CO2. 0.2 kg a year, set against an average person's 4.7 tonnes, works as a permission slip. It also leaves out training, chips, and the growth that ChatGPT use drives across the system.
issues.fix: Add a sourced world CO2 figure for data centres next to the personal figure (the IEA publishes one in Energy and AI), and say the IEA projects it to grow. In my-year, add a line saying this counts only answering your questions, not training, chips or building data centres.

issues.where: Share text (template.html line 320) and reveal copy
issues.problem: The copy-to-share line for one-question spreads 'about 0.34 Wh, by OpenAI's own figure' with no world total. The most viral sentence Hum produces is an OpenAI figure. The bottle card's share text also reads 'NO. No: 10 to 50…', saying no twice.
issues.fix: Add the world clause to every share text ('…; all data centres: more than France, doubling by 2030'). Drop the stamp prefix when the result already starts with the verdict word.

issues.where: Bigger picture box under the card, and the world clause on the power-mix answer
issues.problem: 'The IEA expects renewables to meet half of the growth' is good news on its face, and its other half goes unsaid: the rest of the growth comes mostly from gas and coal. The 'bigger picture' is also styled as a footnote under the reveal, smaller than the trivia.
issues.fix: Say both halves: 'renewables meet about half the growth; the rest comes largely from gas and coal' (source the second half or drop the claim). Give the bigger picture equal visual weight with the answer on the reveal.

keep: Quotes are shown verbatim and marked 'Quote checked on the page' with a date. That is the site's credibility, and no industry PR does it.
The 'COMPANY SAYS SO' tag on every company figure. Make it even more visible.
The 'What nobody knows yet' fold, especially 'OpenAI hasn't published how its 0.34 Wh is measured'. Bring that line up into the main answer.
The world clause on every answer (485 TWh, more than France, doubling by 2030).
The power-mix card's answer, 'Coal, at about 30%', and its distinction between the grid a data centre draws from and what companies buy on paper.
Drafts are clearly labelled 'Draft' with a dashed box. Honest about what isn't reviewed.
The bills answer names PJM and the independent market monitor and says these are estimates, not measured bills.
The calc lines that show Hum's own arithmetic; they let me check the work.
reviews.persona: a climate activist who worries the site lets the industry off the hook

reviews.first_10_seconds: A myth-checker for AI's electricity, water and CO2 that says every number is sourced. I can tell what it's for right away. My next move is to check whether its quick comparisons actually hold up.
reviews.verdict: The structure is better than most energy explainers I review. It names consumption explicitly, separates the grid a data centre draws from with what companies buy on paper, and calls the PJM market monitor's numbers estimates rather than measured bills. The "what nobody knows" folds are honest. But I would not forward it yet. The first thing a visitor sees, the guess card, marks the wrong answer as correct. "A few seconds of a phone charge" is off by more than an order of magnitude: 0.34 Wh is about a minute or more of charging. The flight page calls a CO2e figure that includes non-CO2 warming effects "CO2". The "more than France" line repeated on every page claims a 0.9% margin between two figures measured on different boundaries. The range bar ranks Google, OpenAI and a Llama estimate as low/mid/high even though they measure different things, which breaks Hum's own rule. The emissions-accounting pages also skip the market-based versus location-based distinction, and that distinction is the whole story behind Google's and Microsoft's numbers. Fix these and I would share it with colleagues. Ship as is and the first grid person who reads it will screenshot the phone-charge card.

issues.where: Front door and Today guess card (q002 guess.options[0], right: 0)
issues.problem: The card marks "A few seconds of a phone charge" as the right answer, and that is arithmetically wrong. One phone charge is about 19 Wh (EPA) and takes 1.5 to 2 hours at roughly 10 to 15 W. So 0.34 Wh is 1.8% of a charge, about 80 to 120 seconds of charging. At the 1.86 Wh high end it is about 6 to 10 minutes. "Seconds" belongs to Altman's oven comparison (about 1 kW), not to a phone. The reveal then says "Less than a phone charge", which doesn't match the option either. This is the first number every visitor sees.
issues.fix: Change the option to "About a minute of charging a phone" or "About 2% of a phone charge" (0.34 / 19). Add the charger wattage the time is based on as a sourced constant, or drop the time framing and use the fraction. Make the reveal headline match the option, e.g. "Right: about 1/50 of a phone charge".

issues.where: Answer page 'flight' (answer text)
issues.problem: The page says "246 kg of CO2 per passenger", but Our World in Data's 246 g/km for domestic flights is CO2-equivalent from UK government factors, and those include the radiative-forcing uplift for non-CO2 effects at altitude (multiplier about 1.9). Direct CO2 is roughly half that. The page then compares this CO2e figure with a CO2-only per-question figure (0.34 Wh × 473 g/kWh). The 1.5 million and 200,000 ratios are inflated by about 1.9× and the unit is mislabelled.
issues.fix: Call it "246 kg CO2e (including non-CO2 warming at altitude)". Either add the government's CO2-only factor as a second sourced number and recompute (about 0.8 million and 0.12 million questions), or show both. Add the boundary to "What nobody knows" or to the claim fold.

issues.where: Every 'world' clause and the home reveal: "485 TWh in 2025, more than France (481 TWh)"
issues.problem: This is false precision across mismatched boundaries. 485 versus 480.6 TWh is a 0.9% gap. The IEA figure is a modelled estimate with uncertainty far larger than 1%. Ember's "demand" is generation plus net imports, so it includes transmission and distribution losses, while the IEA figure is data-centre final consumption. On a like-for-like basis (French final consumption is about 10% lower) the comparison still roughly holds, but "more than" is not a defensible claim, and it is the site's headline line.
issues.fix: Say "about as much as France uses (481 TWh)". In the sources, note that Ember's demand includes grid losses. If you want an unambiguous "more than", pick a country whose figure is at least 15 to 20% below 485 TWh.

issues.where: Range bar on 'one-question' and 'google-search' (low/mid/high = Google 0.24 / OpenAI 0.34 / MIT TR 1.86)
issues.problem: This breaks Hum's own rule against ranking models across different measurement boundaries. Google's 0.24 Wh is a median that counts idle machines, host CPU and cooling (PUE). OpenAI's 0.34 is an undisclosed "average" with no method. MIT TR's 6,706 J is a Llama 3.1 405B GPU measurement doubled to estimate the full server. Putting them on one axis as low/middle/high, with OpenAI's unexplained number as the "middle", tells the reader these are comparable points in a distribution. They aren't.
issues.fix: Show them as three separate labelled dots without low/mid/high semantics. Tag each with its boundary ("median, incl. idle + cooling", "average, method not published", "one open model, GPU ×2"). Drop the word "middle" and the shaded band between them. The headline can still say "about 0.3 Wh, by the companies' own figures".

issues.where: Answer page 'big-tech-emissions'
issues.problem: The emissions-accounting core is missing. The page cites "scope 2 decreased 3% while electricity use increased 37%" but never explains it: that fall is market-based scope 2, produced by contracts and certificates. The location-based figure almost certainly rose. Hum's own draft says most of the increase is scope 3 (construction and hardware) and that Microsoft partly blamed its change in renewable-certificate accounting. The reviewed page simply says "Both point to building and running more data centres". The 2030 net-zero and carbon-negative targets have no quote in the sources.
issues.fix: Add one sentence: "Google's scope 2 fell 3% because it counts clean-power contracts (market-based); the grid it physically draws from wasn't 37% cleaner." Add one line saying most of the rise is scope 3 (building data centres and chips). Bring in Microsoft's certificate-accounting change from the draft with its quote. Source the 2030 targets or remove them. Link to power-mix for the paper versus physical point.

issues.where: Answer page 'power-mix' (result "Coal, at about 30%"; also shown as the badge in the home list)
issues.problem: The question is "coal, gas or renewables?" and the headline answers "Coal". The same IEA data gives renewables plus nuclear at 42% low-carbon against 56% fossil (coal 30 + gas 26). "Coal" is technically the largest single source but is a misleading one-word verdict. As a badge in the topic list it reads like a stamp. The 30/27/26/15 split also comes from the 2025 Energy and AI report, while the world clause uses the 2026 Key Questions report, without saying so.
issues.fix: Headline: "Mostly fossil: about 56% coal and gas, 42% renewables and nuclear (IEA)". Keep "coal is the largest single source" in the body. Use a proper verdict badge format in the list, not free text. Name the report edition and its base year (2024) next to the split.

issues.where: Answer page 'bills', its world clause, and the PJM/Ireland drafts
issues.problem: The page says "one capacity auction" without naming it; it was the July 2025 base auction for 2026/27. The 9% / $10.48/MWh has no period (the draft says "through July 2026"). The world clause says "Outside places like PJM and Ireland, Hum has no sourced figure", which implies a sourced Ireland bill figure, but Hum's own Ireland draft concludes the bill effect is unknown. The drafts also contradict each other. One says the December 2025 auction was about 6,600 MW short and another says about 6,500 MW. One says $333/MW-day was "nine times the 2024/25 price", but the 2024/25 RTO price was about $28.92, so the ratio is about 11.5×. Nine times is the 2025/26 jump.
issues.fix: Name the auction ("2026/27 base auction, held July 2025") and the period behind the 9% figure. Change the world clause to "Outside PJM, Hum has no sourced figure for the bill effect". Run a consistency pass across the PJM drafts: one shortfall number per auction and ratios recomputed from sourced clearing prices. Add the clearing prices as sourced constants rather than prose.

issues.where: Flight, my-year, ladder, world-share
issues.problem: There are several small accounting gaps. (1) Ember's 473 g/kWh is generation intensity, applied to data-centre consumption without the roughly 5 to 8% grid losses, and it is a 2024 figure used next to 2025 numbers. (2) The "4.7 tonnes per person" divides 38.1 Gt by a world population that isn't sourced anywhere. (3) The kettle's "99 Wh at the very least" assumes water starting at 15°C (85 K × 4.184 kJ); from 20°C it is 93 Wh, so "at least" isn't a floor, and the starting temperature isn't stated. (4) The world-share page splices 415 TWh (2024, 2025 edition) with 485 TWh (2025, 2026 edition) as "it grew to", which mixes report vintages that may have revised 2024. (5) My-year applies a per-query figure to "messages".
issues.fix: State "generation intensity, grid losses not included" in the CO2 sums, or add a sourced loss factor. Source the population figure. State the kettle's starting temperature (e.g. 20°C, about 93 Wh) and drop "at the very least". Use the 2026 report's own 2024 value for the growth comparison, or say the figures come from different editions. Note that messages are being treated as queries.

keep: Saying "consumption" explicitly ("counts electricity consumed, not generated"). It is rare and correct.
The power-mix page separates the physical grid a data centre draws from with what companies buy on paper. Push this into the big-tech page too.
Bills: "These are the monitor's estimates, not measured bills" and "depends on your utility and state". This is exactly the right caveat for capacity-market numbers.
The Netflix page admits the boundary mismatch (2019 figure, includes your device, versus data centre only).
The claim marker on the Google-search range bar (2.9 Wh shown against today's figures) makes the 'out of date' point visually.
"What nobody knows yet" folds, e.g. OpenAI's unpublished method and no per-search figure since 2009.
Verbatim quotes with 'checked on the page' and the honest flag that the big-tech and bills figures come from trade-press reports of the primary documents.
Clear 'Draft' labelling on unreviewed answers.
Water: tracing the 'bottle per email' myth back to Li et al.'s 10 to 50 responses per 500 ml, and noting the split between on-site water and water at the power stations.
reviews.persona: an energy-systems analyst (grids, capacity markets, emissions accounting) checking the technical claims

reviews.first_10_seconds: A myth-busting desk for AI's energy, water and CO2: it says "every number sourced" and lets me guess before it rules. The pitch is fact-checking. That means I'll judge it the way I'd judge a fact-check: does each verdict match the evidence, and is each number right?
reviews.verdict: The way the sourcing is built is better than most newsroom fact-checks. Quotes are copied word for word and marked "checked on the page", company claims are labelled, the sums are shown, and the "What nobody knows yet" fold is something we should copy. The verdicts are a different matter. The very first thing a visitor sees is a factual error: the "right" answer, "a few seconds of a phone charge", understates the figure by about 20 to 40 times. Several verdict stamps say more than their own evidence does. The big-tech page says YES "because of AI" while its own unknowns admit neither company separates AI from other work. The Google page puts PARTLY next to a body that says "roughly similar, not proven". The water page says NO without having read the claim's actual origin. The range bar sets Google's median, OpenAI's unexplained average and a GPU-only lab measurement side by side as low, middle and high, which breaks Hum's own rule against comparing figures measured differently. One "unknown" (where the IEA's 2.9 Wh came from) looks traceable. The verdict scale also leaks: results like "Coal, at about 30%" sit in the stamp column, an "OUT OF DATE" chip is styled like a second verdict, and the 299 drafts carry free-text verdicts in public. I wouldn't put my name to sharing this until the guess card is fixed and each stamp is checked against its own answer text. Fix those and the method is genuinely strong.

issues.where: Home and Today guess card, q002 guess.right=0 'A few seconds of a phone charge' (reviewed.py line 57)
issues.problem: Wrong by an order of magnitude. Your own figures put 0.34 Wh at about 1/56 of a 19 Wh charge (1.8%). A phone takes roughly 1 to 2 hours to charge at about 5 to 20 W, so 0.34 Wh is about 1 to 4 minutes of charging, not seconds. At the high figure (1.86 Wh) it is about 10% of a charge. This is the first claim every visitor sees, and it would be the first correction notice.
issues.fix: Change the correct option to 'About 1/50th of a phone charge' or 'A minute or two of phone charging'. Add the sum to calc ('19 Wh ÷ 0.34 Wh ≈ 56'). Add a build check that recomputes every guess option's ratio from the source figures.

issues.where: Google-search myth page, 'What nobody knows yet': 'The IEA didn't publish how it got 2.9 Wh.'
issues.problem: This looks false. IEA Electricity 2024 footnotes the 2.9 Wh to de Vries (2023, Joule), which derives it from SemiAnalysis estimates of ChatGPT's daily energy and request volume. The derivation is traceable, just weak. Calling it unknown is itself an unsourced claim, on the page that sets out to debunk an unsourced claim.
issues.fix: Open the IEA PDF's footnote, then replace the line with something like: 'The 2.9 Wh came from a 2023 estimate by Alex de Vries, built on analysts' guesses about ChatGPT's servers, not a measurement.' Add de Vries as a source with a checked quote.

issues.where: Big tech emissions page: stamp YES, 'Yes, by their own reports'
issues.problem: The stamp says more than the evidence. The question is about cause ('because of AI'), yet the page's own unknowns say 'Neither company separates AI from its other data-centre work'. The companies attribute the rise to data-centre building, and Google's scope 2 fell 3%, so the growth is largely supply chain and construction. The figures also come second-hand from trade-press reports Hum hasn't checked against the original reports. YES needs first-hand evidence that answers the question as asked.
issues.fix: Change the stamp to PARTLY with the result 'Data centres, yes; AI specifically, they don't say'. Keep the 'company figures' chip. Allow no YES or NO on a claim until the primary report has been read on the page.

issues.where: Range bars on one-question and google-search pages ('from 0.24 (Google (Gemini)) to 1.86 (large open model), middle 0.34 (OpenAI)')
issues.problem: This ranks figures measured in different ways, which Hum's own rules forbid. Google's 0.24 is a median that counts idle machines and overhead. OpenAI's 0.34 is an unexplained average from a CEO blog post. The 1.86 is MIT Technology Review's GPU measurement on Llama 405B, doubled. 'Middle' suggests a central estimate when it is simply the company figure that happens to fall between the other two. On the Google page, 'about ten times lower than 2.9 Wh' quotes only the low end, while the bar's top (1.86) is only 1.6 times lower.
issues.fix: Drop 'low / middle / high'. Show three separate labelled markers, each with its measurement scope in a few words (e.g. 'Google median, counts idle machines' / 'OpenAI average, scope unpublished' / 'lab test, chips only'). Rewrite the Google answer as: 'Newer published figures run from 0.24 to 1.86 Wh, between about 1.5 and 12 times lower than 2.9 Wh.'

issues.where: Google myth stamp PARTLY plus 'OUT OF DATE' chip; home 'bigger picture' row showing 'Coal, at about 30%' in the stamp column; drafts with free-text verdicts
issues.problem: The verdict scale isn't held to. The PARTLY stamp conflicts with the body ('roughly similar, not proven', meaning the 10x is no longer supported). The OUT OF DATE chip is drawn like a second stamp. A non-verdict result sits in the verdict column. The 299 public drafts carry their own wording ('Probably not any more', 'Mostly not'). Readers can't learn what each stamp means if it keeps changing.
issues.fix: Publish a one-screen rating guide that defines YES, PARTLY, NO, NOBODY KNOWS and OUTDATED, and link it from every stamp. Rate the Google myth OUTDATED (or NO) as the only stamp. In the stamp column, show a stamp only for claim pages and put 'how much' results in the subtitle line. Hide draft verdict sentences behind 'Draft notes', or show no verdict at all until reviewed.

issues.where: Bottle-of-water page: stamp NO; unknowns admit 'A newspaper figure of about a bottle per 100-word email (GPT-4) circulates, but Hum couldn't read it on the page'
issues.problem: The viral 'bottle per email' line comes mainly from the 2024 Washington Post/UC Riverside piece about GPT-4 and a 100-word email, not the GPT-3 per-answer range. Answering NO to the version Hum could read, while setting aside the actual source, is rebutting a weaker version of the claim. Comparing a study range that includes power-station water with company figures that may leave it out is also mixing measurement scopes.
issues.fix: Get the Washington Post figure checked (archive or the UCR authors' own write-up) before rating. Until then, stamp it NOBODY KNOWS or PARTLY, with a result like 'Depends which model and which water you count'.

issues.where: WORLD clause on every page: '485 TWh in 2025, more than France (481 TWh)'
issues.problem: This claims a ranking from a 0.9% gap between two different kinds of number: an IEA modelled estimate of data-centre consumption and Ember's measured national demand, which includes grid losses. The IEA estimate's own uncertainty is far bigger than 4 TWh. 'More than France' is false precision that a careful reader will catch.
issues.fix: Say 'about as much electricity as France (481 TWh)'. Add a rule: comparisons of the form 'more than X' need a gap larger than the stated uncertainty.

issues.where: 'How big is that?' ladder and flight page
issues.problem: 'about 1× the rung above' (99 vs 90 Wh) says nothing. '99 Wh at the very least' for 1 litre assumes a start temperature it doesn't state (from 20°C the floor is about 93 Wh). 'One short AI video clip 90 Wh' generalises from one small open model (WAN2.1 1.3B). The flight's 246 g/km from Our World in Data is a UK-government CO2-equivalent factor that, I believe, includes non-CO2 warming effects, yet the page calls it 'kg of CO2'. The card's 'Boiling a kettle' option and the ladder's '1 litre' also don't match.
issues.fix: Write 'about the same' when a ratio is under 1.5. Show the kettle sum with its start temperature. Relabel the video rung 'one short clip from a small open model'. Check the OWID footnote and write 'CO2e (including contrails' warming)' if that's what the factor is. Use '1 litre in a kettle' on the card.

keep: Verbatim quotes with 'Quote checked on the page' and a date. This is better than most professional fact-checks.
Company figures labelled 'COMPANY SAYS SO' / 'company figures', separate from estimates and measurements
The 'What nobody knows yet' fold. Saying openly what is unknown builds trust.
The 'Why the claim misleads' line naming how a claim got distorted (e.g. a bottle per 10 to 50 answers retold as a bottle per answer)
The claim quoted at the top with where it circulates ('heard from'), before the verdict
Sums shown in calc (Netflix 77 ÷ 0.34 ≈ 230, flight 1.5 million and 236,000, my-year 0.46 kWh ≈ 0.22 kg). I checked them and they are correct.
Saying plainly that the bills and big-tech pages rely on trade-press reports of the primary documents
Drafts clearly marked 'Draft' with a dashed note, kept apart from reviewed answers
The guess-then-reveal format, once the correct answers themselves are correct
reviews.persona: a professional fact-checker (Full Fact / AFP style) judging the verdict method and wording

reviews.first_10_seconds: VoiceOver opens on the tab title "Hum Answers prototype". Then it reads the ribbon, which sits outside any landmark, then "Hum, home", Today, Search. The heading "AI's electricity, water and CO2: straight answers, every number sourced" tells me what the site is for: a place to check AI energy claims. It's clear enough and I'd stay. Then I swipe into the card and hear "One short ChatGPT question uses about as much electricity as…" read as plain text, not a heading, followed by four "toggle buttons, not pressed". That's a quiz pretending to be a set of switches.
reviews.verdict: The foundations are better than most prototypes I'm handed. It uses Atkinson Hyperlegible, real buttons, native details/summary folds, 44px+ targets, a visible focus ring, a reduced-motion rule, and polite live regions for the search count and "Copied". Focus moves to the reveal heading after a guess, and every range bar has a text caption. But the parts that make this product different don't work for me. After a guess, the only way to see which option was right is a cream border instead of an amber one (1.74:1 between them). The buttons claim to be toggles. "Next question" rebuilds the whole page and drops me on a button without ever reading me the new question. Changing pages never changes the title and never announces the new heading. The range bar is read twice, and its axis labels render at about 6px on a phone. The search field's border is 1.46:1 against the page, so low-vision users can barely find the main way in. On top of that, the first thing every visitor sees has a factual error: the "right" answer, "A few seconds of a phone charge", is wrong by more than ten times. I'd share the reviewed answer pages once the routing and the quiz semantics are fixed. Right now I wouldn't send a blind friend to the home page.

issues.where: Home card 1 / Today card: reviewed.py line 57, guess options, right=0
issues.problem: The correct answer is given as "A few seconds of a phone charge". Hum's own figures say 0.34 Wh against a 19 Wh charge (US EPA), which is about 1.8% of a charge. A phone takes roughly 1.5 to 2 hours to fill, so that's about 1 to 2 minutes of charging, not seconds. At the 1.86 Wh high end it's about 10% of a charge. No source in the answer gives a charging time, so "seconds" is unsourced and wrong by more than ten times. This is the first thing every visitor sees, and the reveal then says "Less than a phone charge", which doesn't match the option.
issues.fix: Use options that come straight from sourced numbers, e.g. "About 2% of a phone charge" (0.34 ÷ 19, shown in Hum's sums), "A whole phone charge", "Boiling a kettle", "A day of a fridge". Make the result line match: "About 1/50 of a phone charge." If you want a time, source a charger wattage and add the sum.

issues.where: bindCard() in template.html: choice buttons after a guess
issues.problem: The correct option is shown only by colour: a cream border and text instead of amber (1.74:1 between them, failing WCAG 1.4.1). It has no text or icon. aria-pressed turns every option into a "toggle button", which is the wrong role for a one-shot answer. Every button is then set to disabled, so a screen reader user can't go back through the options to find which was right. Colour-blind and low-vision sighted users can't tell either.
issues.fix: Remove aria-pressed. After a guess, use aria-disabled="true" instead of disabled so the buttons stay in the reading order. Add visible text to them: append " ✓ Right answer" to the correct one and " · Your guess" to the chosen one, with the icon aria-hidden and the words in the DOM. Style the right one with a check icon and a solid fill, not just a different border.

issues.where: route() / main.focus() / document title
issues.problem: It's a single-page app built on hash routes, but document.title never changes (it's "Hum Answers prototype" on every view). Focus goes to an unnamed <main tabindex=-1>, so on most screen readers navigating to an answer, topic or Today is either silent or reads the whole region. That fails WCAG 2.4.2 and 4.1.3 in practice. The "Just tell me" link and every list link fire this silent navigation.
issues.fix: In each view, set document.title = `${question} · Hum`. Give each view's h1 tabindex="-1" and focus it (instead of main) after rendering. Keep a polite live region in the header that announces the new page's h1.

issues.where: Home: "Next question" handler (home() re-render)
issues.problem:
