"Next question" rebuilds the entire home page with innerHTML, wipes whatever the user typed in search, and focuses the first choice button. A screen reader user hears "Whole phone charge, button" and never hears the new question. The card prompt is also a

rather than a heading, and the reveal uses an h3 directly under the page h1, so the heading outline skips a level and there's no heading to jump to.
issues.fix: Re-render only #card. Make the prompt an <h2 class="claim" tabindex="-1"> and focus it on Next, so the question is read first and the options follow. Make the reveal heading an h3 under that h2 (now valid). Add visually hidden text to the progress dots: "Question 2 of 11".

issues.where: rangeSvg() / rangeBlock(): every range bar
issues.problem: The SVG has role=img with an aria-label that repeats the caption paragraph right below it, so screen readers read the same long sentence twice. The caption's last clause also comes out as a lowercase fragment: "…middle 0.34 (OpenAI). the 2.9 Wh behind “10×”." Visually, the 12-unit SVG text is scaled from a 600-wide viewBox into a roughly 300px card, so labels like 0.24, 1.86 and "the 2.9 Wh behind 10×" render at about 6px (see the reveal and answer-page screenshots). The band fill is 1.26:1 against the card, so in practice only the dashed stroke shows the range.
issues.fix: Mark the SVG aria-hidden="true" and let the caption carry the meaning. Rewrite claimNote as a full sentence: "The claim used 2.9 Wh (IEA 2024)." Either draw the low/mid/high labels as HTML under the bar, or raise the SVG font size to about 24 units so they're at least 12px at 375px. Make the band fill visibly lighter (≥3:1 against the surface).

issues.where: .search input (home, the main way in)
issues.problem: The search field's border (#2A3038) is 1.46:1 against the page and its fill is 1.12:1, failing WCAG 1.4.11 non-text contrast. In the screenshots it reads as a faint grey rectangle. This is the product's main entry point, and low-vision users can't find its edges. Focus also replaces the outline with a 1.5px border colour change, which is weak.
issues.fix: Give the input a border of at least 3:1, e.g. var(--muted) #9BA1AD (5.1:1 on rule, about 7:1 on night), and keep the cream border plus an outline (or a 2px border) on focus. Do the same for .btn.quiet ("Next question"), whose border is also --rule.

issues.where: Verdict stamps and row tags (ICON map), details summaries
issues.problem: Decorative glyphs are read aloud. "✓ YES" becomes "check mark YES", and "◐ PARTLY" becomes "circle with left half black PARTLY". On home and topic rows the whole link name gets long: question, then icon, then verdict, then sub-line. The summary::after content "+" / "–" is read by VoiceOver as "plus" / "en dash" after every fold name, on top of the native expanded/collapsed state.
issues.fix: Wrap the icons in <span aria-hidden="true">. Write the stamp as "Hum's verdict: Partly" in the DOM, with the visible order unchanged. Use content: "+" / ""; (CSS alt text) on summary::after. For the units, add <abbr title="watt-hours">Wh</abbr> once per page, or spell out "watt-hours" in captions, because "W h" and "T W h" mean nothing when spoken.

issues.where: Sticky header, page shell
issues.problem: The sticky header (about 57px) has no scroll-padding, so when you Shift+Tab back through long answer pages, focused links and summaries end up hidden under it (WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured). There's no lang attribute in the template, so screen readers guess the voice. The prototype ribbon sits outside any landmark.
issues.fix: Add html { scroll-padding-top: 72px; }, set <html lang="en-GB"> (or document.documentElement.lang at startup), and either put the ribbon inside <header> or give it role="note".

keep: Atkinson Hyperlegible Next and Mono as the body and number fonts: the right choice for low vision and dyslexia
A range-bar caption in text on every chart, and log-scale ladder bars marked aria-hidden with the value written out in text
Native <details>/<summary> folds (they get expanded state for free) and real <button type=button> elements
Focus moving to the reveal heading after a guess, and polite live regions for the search count and "Copied"
44 to 52px touch targets, a :focus-visible outline in cream (high contrast), and the prefers-reduced-motion rule
Muted text at 6.7:1 or better and amber at 9.95:1: body text contrast is solid
role=search with a real <label for=q> (not a placeholder-only label), and the honest "No answer yet" result
A readonly textarea for the share text with a copy-and-select fallback: works without the clipboard API
reviews.persona: an accessibility specialist who uses a screen reader and checks WCAG (read the source for semantics, focus, contrast)

reviews.first_10_seconds: OK, it is something about AI and electricity and water. "Straight answers, every number sourced" I understand. Then there is a quiz about ChatGPT and a kettle. I don't really use a kettle, but I can guess. I think it is a site that tells you if things you hear about AI and energy are true. Everything is about America though: US home, Virginia, PJM, my bill. That is not my bill.
reviews.verdict: The quiz card works. I tapped before I had decided to, and the reveal with the world total ("more than France") is the first moment I understood why this matters. That part is good. Then problems started. The answer the site calls correct, "A few seconds of a phone charge", is wrong by its own numbers: 0.34 Wh out of a 19 Wh charge is about 2% of a full charge, which is a minute or more of charging, not seconds. A fact-checking site cannot get its first card wrong. After that, the numbers are written the English way: "28,000 Wh" reads to me as twenty-eight watt-hours, and "0.34" as a typo. The slashed zeros in the mono font look like the letter Ø. Almost everything after the first card is about the US: US home, US EPA, PJM, Virginia, Dominion. Only one of 310 answers mentions Brazil, and the bills question ("is AI raising my bill?") has nothing to say about my bill. Some phrases I had to read twice: "the rung above", "folds", "Why the claim misleads", "Just tell me". The page is about 800 KB because all 299 drafts are loaded on the first screen, and fonts come from Google, so it is slow on prepaid data. Sharing means copying text from a box, but I share in WhatsApp with one tap. I would stay for two or three cards. I would not come back, because none of it is about where I live, and I would not forward it to my family, who would not understand "Wh".

issues.where: Home card 1 (reviewed.py guess options, right=0) and the reveal
issues.problem: The 'correct' option, 'A few seconds of a phone charge', contradicts the site's own figures. 0.34 Wh / 19 Wh is about 1.8% of a full charge, which is roughly 1 to 4 minutes on a 5 to 20 W charger. At the 1.86 Wh high end it is about 10% of a charge. Calling that 'seconds' is an order-of-magnitude error, and it sits in the first thing every visitor sees.
issues.fix: Change the option to 'About 2% of one phone charge' or 'A minute or two of charging', and add the calculation line '0.34 Wh ÷ 19 Wh ≈ 1.8%' to the card's calc. Rewrite the reveal headline to say what is true ('About 2% of a phone charge'), not just 'Less than a phone charge'.

issues.where: All numbers (fmt() and lab() use toLocaleString('en-GB'); ladder, range bar, prose)
issues.problem: In Brazil, and in most of Europe and Latin America, '28,000 Wh' means 28 Wh and '0.34' looks wrong. Readers outside English-speaking countries will misread the ladder by a factor of 1,000. The Atkinson Mono slashed zero also looks like Ø to people who do not read code.
issues.fix: Avoid thousands separators in prose and ladders: write '28 kWh' or '28 thousand Wh'. Format with navigator.language, or at least use a thin space for thousands. Use the proportional body font for numbers inside sentences and keep mono only for the bar labels.

issues.where: Ladder (US home, US EPA), Bills topic (PJM, Virginia, Maryland, Dominion), search placeholder 'is AI raising my bill?'
issues.problem: The comparisons and the bills shelf are almost all American. Only 1 of 310 answers mentions Brazil, and 73 mention India against 117 for Virginia. A visitor outside the US is promised 'my bill' and gets PJM capacity auctions, so they learn nothing about their own country.
issues.fix: Use global comparisons in the ladder, such as 'an average home in the world for a day' or 'a fridge for a day', with a world or IEA source. Give the bills answer a first line that says the evidence so far is mostly from the US and Ireland. Add a 'Where you live' shelf even if it is short, and list Brazil, India, the EU and others as 'nobody has published this yet' when that is the truth.

issues.where: Answer page and card reveal share box (template.html lines 298 and 336)
issues.problem: 'Copy to share' copies text from a readonly textarea. On a cheap Android phone, people share with the system share sheet straight to WhatsApp. Copying and pasting is two extra steps, and the box takes up a third of the screen.
issues.fix: Use navigator.share({title, text, url}) when it is available, with one button labelled 'Send' or 'Share'. Fall back to copying only when it is not. Hide the textarea behind the button.

issues.where: Page weight (index.html is about 818 KB, with drafts.json inlined; Google Fonts with 3 families)
issues.problem: The first screen downloads all 299 drafts and three web-font families before it is useful. On 3G or prepaid data and a slow CPU, that is several seconds of blank or unstyled page, which works against the founder's goal of keeping visitors past the first minute.
issues.fix: Ship the front door with only the card deck and the search index (questions and slugs, about 30 KB). Load each draft's body when someone opens it. Self-host one subset font, or use the system font for the body text.

issues.where: Ladder 'about N× the rung above'; range caption 'the 2.9 Wh behind "10×".'
issues.problem: 'Rung' is a word most non-native readers do not know. 'about 1× the rung above' (99 Wh vs 90 Wh) says nothing. The range caption has a lowercase fragment, 'the 2.9 Wh behind "10×".', that is not a sentence.
issues.fix: Write 'about 5 times the line above', and leave the line out when the ratio is under 2 ('about the same as above'). Rewrite the caption as: 'The old 2.9 Wh figure behind the "10 times" claim is shown by the dotted line.'

issues.where: Home: callout titled 'The bigger picture' followed directly by a section h2 also titled 'The bigger picture'
issues.problem: Two blocks one after the other have the same heading but different content, a world total and then a list of questions. That is confusing, and when I translated it, it read as a repeat.
issues.fix: Rename the list to 'Questions people ask most' and keep 'The bigger picture' only for the world-total callout.

issues.where: Search (search() strips non a-z characters; no Portuguese)
issues.problem: Accented words are split up ('água' becomes 'gua'). A query like 'conta de luz' or 'ChatGPT gasta água' gets nothing or random results, and the message 'On the real site this would tell Hum what to write next' only helps English speakers.
issues.fix: Normalise accents with NFD and strip diacritics before matching, and add a small synonym list for the top terms (água/water, luz/conta/bill, energia/electricity). The empty state should say plainly that Hum answers in English for now.

keep: The guess-first card. It is the only part I used without thinking, and it makes the number stick.
The world total after the reveal, '485 TWh, more than France'. A comparison to a country is understood in any language. Keep it, and maybe let readers choose the country.
Verdict stamps with symbols (PARTLY with a half-circle, YES with a tick). I can read these without good English.
The 'What nobody knows yet' fold. It makes me trust the site more than the confident answers do.
Verbatim source quotes with 'checked on the page' and the date, plus the labels 'Company says so' and 'Estimated'.
A clear dashed 'Draft' box on unreviewed answers.
Large tap targets (52 px choices) and good contrast on the dark background, which work on a cheap screen in sunlight.
'No sign-up' on the Today page.
reviews.persona: a non-native English speaker in Brazil reading on a cheap Android phone

reviews.first_10_seconds: A dark, serious page that says "AI's electricity, water and CO2: straight answers, every number sourced," then a search box and a quiz card. I get it: a fact-checker for AI energy claims, with a game on top. But the first thing I read is a grey "Prototype for testing…draft…" strip, and the headline never says "data centres" or why I should care. The quiz card is what keeps me. I'd tap a guess within 5 seconds, so the front door mostly works. Once I scroll past the card, though, it reads like a blog's archive list, not an app.
reviews.verdict: This is a real step up from "visitors don't know what it's for". The guess-then-reveal card is the right hook, and the answer pages are the most honest AI-energy explainers I've seen: verdict stamp, the claim quoted, sources with checked quotes, "what nobody knows yet". But the hook's own right answer is factually wrong. 0.34 Wh is about 1/56 of a 19 Wh phone charge, so a minute or two of charging, not "a few seconds". On a site whose whole promise is "every number sourced", that is a blocker, and so is a reveal headline ("Less than a phone charge") that doesn't name the option it marked correct. After the reveal, momentum collapses into long text: a second section also called "The bigger picture", a plain list of rows, and a Today page that shows the same card as the home page. It feels like an app for 20 seconds and like a blog after that. I wouldn't share it yet. The share moment (score plus line) only exists on Today, and the card I'd want to send has no share button. Fix the number, make the loop guess, reveal, share, next, and push the long text down.

issues.where: Home and Today guess card, option 0 (reviewed.py line 57, right=0)
issues.problem: The option marked correct, 'A few seconds of a phone charge', is wrong by Hum's own numbers. 0.34 Wh ÷ 19 Wh ≈ 1.8% of a charge, which is roughly 1 to 2 minutes of charging. At the top of the range (1.86 Wh) it is about 10% of a charge, around 10 minutes. The very first fact a visitor meets doesn't survive a check.
issues.fix: Change the option to 'About a minute of charging a phone' (or 'About 1/50 of a phone charge') and put the sum in calc: '19 Wh ÷ 0.34 Wh ≈ 56 questions per charge'. Better still, word every option as a fraction or multiple of one thing (1/50 of a phone charge, a whole charge, a kettle, a fridge day) so the answer can be derived from sourced figures, not timing guesses.

issues.where: Reveal headline (template.html line 233, result field)
issues.problem: The reveal says 'Not quite. Less than a phone charge.' but doesn't name the option it marked correct, so the guess gets no closure. The selected wrong answer stays filled orange while the right one gets only a faint outline (screenshot 2), so the eye reads the kettle as the 'answer'.
issues.fix: Headline: 'It's the first one: about 1/50 of a phone charge.' Mark the right option with a solid fill and a tick, and dim the wrong pick with a cross. Put the number (0.34 Wh) in the headline at large size, above the range bar.

issues.where: Home below the card and the in-card callout
issues.problem: 'The bigger picture' appears twice in a row: as the callout inside the reveal and as the H2 of the list below. The list is then mixed rows with stamps (YES/PARTLY) next to free-text results ('Coal, at about 30%') set in the same stamp style. It reads as a blog index, and the hierarchy is lost.
issues.fix: Rename the section to 'Questions people ask' and show stamps only. Move non-verdict results ('Coal, at about 30%', 'About 1.5%') into the sub line in body type, with no caps-mono stamp. Better still, show the next 3 playable cards as horizontally swipeable tiles so the home page stays an app.

issues.where: Answer page, 'How big is that?' ladder
issues.problem: The bars are on a log scale, but lay readers read bar length linearly. A US home for a day (28 kWh) draws about twice as long as a phone charge (19 Wh) when it is about 1,500x bigger. The small caption saying 'log scale' won't be read by a teenager. The comparison chart defeats its own purpose. The same applies to the unlabeled log range bar, where 2.9 Wh sits just beyond 1.86.
issues.fix: Drop bar lengths in the ladder. Use the 'about 56x the rung above' multiplier as the hero of each rung (large, accent colour) with the value on the right, or use a dot-count/icon unit. On the range bar, label the axis 'log scale' inline, or switch to a linear scale with a break.

issues.where: Answer page header, 'OUT OF DATE' chip beside 'PARTLY Hum's verdict'
issues.problem: Two stamps side by side, both boxed. 'OUT OF DATE' reads as if Hum's own page is stale, not the claim. In the first 10 seconds on a shared link, a visitor may conclude the site is out of date.
issues.fix: Make one stamp only: 'PARTLY: the claim uses out-of-date figures'. Or label the second chip 'Claim is out of date' and give it the claim's styling (under the quoted claim), not the verdict's.

issues.where: Card reveal and answer page (no share on card); Today page
issues.problem: The only shareable artefact (Hum #n score line) is on Today, and Today shows the exact same card as the home page (#142 = the ChatGPT phone-charge card), so Today has no reason to exist and the home card can't be shared. 'Would you send any of this?' is the test question, and the answer path isn't there.
issues.fix: Add 'Share this' to every reveal with a pre-written line ('I guessed a kettle. One ChatGPT question is ~1/50 of a phone charge. humearth.org/…'). Make Today a different card from the home default (home rotates or starts at a non-Today card) and show the streak/number prominently.

issues.where: Top ribbon on every page
issues.problem: 'Prototype for testing… Answers marked draft aren't reviewed yet' is the very first text on every screen and uses up the top 70px of the first 10 seconds. It primes distrust before the promise.
issues.fix: For user tests, move it into the footer or a small 'Prototype' pill beside the logo. The Draft label on draft pages already does the honest work.

issues.where: Hero headline and draft answer pages
issues.problem: The headline names AI but not data centres, and it gives no stakes. Draft pages put a bold summary and then a long run of dense paragraphs with no stamp, range bar or folds, so they feel like blog posts and they make up 299 of 310 pages.
issues.fix: Hero: 'How much electricity, water and CO2 does AI really use? Straight answers, every number sourced.' On draft pages, at least show the one-line answer in the same verdict-block layout and fold the body text under 'Read the detail', so drafts look like the same app.

issues.where: Range bar caption on Google-myth page
issues.problem: The caption has a broken sentence: '…middle 0.34 (OpenAI). the 2.9 Wh behind "10×".' The lowercase fragment reads as a bug.
issues.fix: Change it to '…middle 0.34 (OpenAI). The dotted line is the 2.9 Wh behind the "10×" claim.'

keep: Guess-first card as the hero: it is the single thing that makes the first 10 seconds work and turns the page into an app
'Heard something? Ask Hum.' search with the example 'is AI raising my bill?': it states the use case in five words
The verdict-stamp system (YES/PARTLY/NO/NOBODY KNOWS) with the claim quoted verbatim underneath
'What nobody knows yet' fold: a rare, trust-building admission that sets Hum apart
Sources fold with verbatim quotes, the 'COMPANY SAYS SO' label and 'Quote checked on the page, date'
The '56x the rung above' multipliers in the ladder: the clearest scale device on the site
'The bigger picture' world-total clause (485 TWh, more than France) attached to every small number
Clear Draft labelling with the dashed box: honest, and visibly different from the reviewed pages
Dark serif and mono type system: it feels considered, not template-y
reviews.persona: a senior product/UX designer judging the first 10 seconds, hierarchy, and whether it feels like an app or a blog

reviews.first_10_seconds: A site that answers how much electricity, water and CO2 AI uses, with sources, and wants me to guess one number first. That part is clear. Then I looked at the network tab: one 818 KB HTML file (214 KB gzipped) and an empty main element until roughly 755 KB of inlined draft JSON has been parsed and a hash router has run.
reviews.verdict: As a prototype for testing whether people understand the product, it does its job. The DOM is light, the CSS is small and sensible, there are no frameworks, the SVG is hand-built and the folds are native details elements. It falls apart as soon as you treat it as the direction for production. The whole product ships in one inline script. 92% of the bytes are draft answers that nobody on the front door ever opens (src quotes alone are 381 KB raw). Nothing renders until all of that has been parsed, and the project's own budget is 90 KB gzipped for first-screen JS. Every view is client-rendered from a hash. That means no HTML for crawlers or link previews, and the share text points to humearth.org/q/slug, a path this architecture doesn't serve. Fonts are a render-blocking third-party Google stylesheet across three families, which also sits badly with "no tracking". The range bar's labels shrink to about 7 px on a phone. The first card the visitor sees also has an arithmetic error in its right answer, and that is a blocker. Fix the data first, then the render path: prerender each reviewed answer as static HTML, keep drafts out of the first load, and self-host subset fonts. Then this becomes a fast site instead of a fast-looking one.

issues.where: reviewed.py one-question guess (options[0], right=0); home card, Today card
issues.problem: The correct answer, "A few seconds of a phone charge", is wrong by Hum's own figures. 0.34 Wh ÷ 19 Wh is about 1.8% of a charge. That is about 61 s even on a 20 W fast charger, and minutes on a 5 W charger. The page's own calc says 10 to 80 questions per charge, which contradicts "a few seconds". This is the first thing every visitor sees.
issues.fix: Change the option to "About 1/50 of a phone charge" (or "A minute or two of charging", plus a calc line of 19 Wh ÷ 0.34 Wh ≈ 56). Add a build check that every guess option's implied ratio is consistent with the bar's low/mid/high.

issues.where: template.html line 153, const DATA = __DATA__ (index.html is 818 KB, 214 KB gzipped)
issues.problem: All 310 drafts (755 KB raw, 199 KB gzipped) are inlined into the only script. The browser must download and parse the entire HTML, then the JS, then JSON.parse the data, then run route(), before main has any content. On a mid-range Android over 4G that is roughly 1.5 to 3 s of blank page under the ribbon, on a site whose problem is people leaving fast. It is more than twice the project's 90 KB gzipped first-screen budget.
issues.fix: Split the data. Inline only the current play card plus a compact search index of q, slug, cat, reviewed and stamp (about 25 KB raw, 6 KB gzipped). Serve each answer as its own JSON or HTML file and fetch it on navigation. The src, answer and gaps fields of the drafts never load on the home page.

issues.where: route() and hash routing; shareText 'humearth.org/q/${slug}'
issues.problem: Every page is rendered client-side from location.hash. With JS off, or for a crawler or a link unfurler (WhatsApp, iMessage, Slack), there are no answer pages at all: no title, no description, no og tags. The copy-to-share text points to /q/slug, a URL this app can't serve, so the core sharing loop has nothing to land on.
issues.fix: Prerender each reviewed answer and each topic to a static /q/<slug>/index.html at build time, the way src/how/render.ts already does for How We Know. Give each page its own title, meta description and og:image. Keep JS only as progressive enhancement for the guess interaction and search.

issues.where: template.html lines 3-5, Google Fonts stylesheet
issues.problem: A render-blocking third-party CSS request loads 3 families and 5 weights from fonts.googleapis.com and gstatic.com. That means two extra origins before the h1 (the likely LCP element, set in Instrument Serif) gets its real face, a visible font swap on the headline, and visitor IPs sent to Google. That last point conflicts with "no tracking".
issues.fix: Self-host woff2 files subset to Latin. Preload only Instrument Serif and Atkinson Next 400. Drop Mono 600 or use font-synthesis. Set size-adjust/ascent-override on the fallback faces so the swap causes no layout shift.

issues.where: rangeSvg(): viewBox 600 wide, text font-size 12/13
issues.problem: The SVG scales from 600 to about 340 px on a 375 px phone, so tick labels render at about 7 px (visible in the reveal screenshot: '0.24', '1.86' and the claim label are unreadable). The claim label uses text-anchor end with overflow visible and can run off the left edge when the claim is below the range.
issues.fix: Render the labels as HTML positioned with left: calc(x%) over a CSS-drawn band, or set the viewBox width to the container width with a ResizeObserver. Use at least 13 px real text. Clamp the claim label inside 0..W with text-anchor chosen by side.

issues.where: bindCard onNext -> home(); route() main.innerHTML on every view
issues.problem: "Next question" re-renders the entire home view through innerHTML. That wipes the user's half-typed search, rebuilds 12 shelf counts (ALL.filter across 310 entries each, 12 times) and the bigger-picture rows, then forces a scrollIntoView, which makes the page jump on phones. Every route change also discards the DOM and resets scroll.
issues.fix: Re-render only the #card node on Next. Precompute the category counts once at load. Keep the search input outside the re-rendered region.

issues.where: today(): Date.UTC(now.getFullYear()...) using local date; n = 142 + day
issues.problem: "The same for everyone" is false across time zones: the card flips at local midnight, not at UTC midnight. The page also starts at "Hum #142" on its first day, a counter that implies 141 earlier days. That is a small invented number on a site whose product is honest numbers. The Today card is also identical to the home card, so a first visitor gets the same question twice.
issues.fix: Use UTC dates (getUTCFullYear and the other UTC getters) and start at #1. Offset the Today index from the home card, or show the home card from a different pool.

issues.where: ladderHtml() 'about N× the rung above'; rangeText() caption
issues.problem: The ladder prints "about 1× the rung above" (kettle 99 Wh vs video 90 Wh), which reads as a bug. The caption builds strings like "(Google (Gemini))" with nested parentheses, and a lowercase "the 2.9 Wh…" sentence after the full stop. Generated text like this is visible on every reviewed page.
issues.fix: Hide the multiplier when it is under 2× (or say "about the same"). Use an em dash or comma instead of parentheses for notes. Capitalise claimNote in the caption.

keep: No framework and no three.js: plain template strings, native details folds, hand-built SVG. The interaction JS minus the data is about 15 KB and fits the budget easily.
The tiny CSS with design tokens on :root, 44 to 52 px touch targets, safe-area padding and the prefers-reduced-motion guard
localStorage wrapped in try/catch and used only for the per-device tally: no accounts, no tracking
The guess-then-reveal card. It costs nothing to render and is the one thing on the page that makes people act.
Search over q and cat only (not the full answer text), so moving to a small prebuilt index is easy
Each source quote rendered next to its link with a provenance label (Company says so, Estimated, and so on)
The range bar's dashed band, which follows the DESIGN.md rule for showing derived or uncertain values
reviews.persona: a front-end performance engineer reading the source (payload size, render path, mobile performance)

reviews.first_10_seconds: From a crawler's point of view, this is one HTML file called "Hum Answers prototype", and every answer is a #fragment that gets built in JavaScript. As a reader I can see the point right away: plain-English fact-checks on AI's electricity, water and CO2, each with its sources. That is exactly the kind of page Google's AI Overviews, Perplexity and ChatGPT search like to cite. But a search engine can't find any of it yet. There is one URL, one generic title, no description and no dates.
reviews.verdict: The content is unusually citable. Each page has a question as the H1, a verdict word, a range with low/mid/high and named sources, verbatim quotes, the sums shown, and company claims labelled as such. Answer engines want exactly that, and few sites on this topic offer it. I re-did the arithmetic on the flight, Netflix, my-year, water and phone-charge pages and it holds: 246 kg ÷ 0.16 g ≈ 1.5 million, 77 ÷ 0.34 ≈ 230, 26 × 52 × 0.34 Wh ≈ 0.46 kWh ≈ 0.22 kg, 19 Wh ÷ 0.24–1.86 Wh ≈ 10–80. The 485 TWh vs France 480.6 TWh comparison is consumption against demand, so like is compared with like. The problem is how the prototype is built. It is one page with hash routing and 300 answers injected as JS data. There are no per-answer URLs, titles, meta descriptions, canonicals, structured data or visible dates. Google drops #fragments, so today the whole thing would index as one URL. The share text already points at humearth.org/q/{slug}, which doesn't exist yet. The spec says prerendered /q/{slug} pages that work without JS. That is the right plan, so the build has to deliver it. Two more things worry me. Every source carries the same hard-coded "checked 18 Oct 2026", drafts included. And 299 unreviewed drafts are ready to go into the index next to the 11 reviewed pages. Fix those and this could be a first-choice citation for "how much energy does ChatGPT use" queries.

issues.where: template.html route() (lines ~374-385); every href="#slug"; share text "humearth.org/q/${e.slug}"
issues.problem: All views use hash routing (#google-search, #topic-water). Crawlers and answer engines ignore fragments, so 11 answers, 299 drafts and 12 topic pages collapse into one indexable URL. Content only exists after JS runs over a 750 KB injected DATA blob. The share/cite string advertises /q/{slug} URLs that the prototype doesn't serve, so any shared link would 404 if it went live in this form.
issues.fix: Ship the spec's static routes before anything goes public: prerender /q/{slug}, /topics/{shelf} and /today to full HTML at build time, with real <a href="/q/slug"> links. Add a sitemap.xml listing only the reviewed /q pages with lastmod. Add a CI check that fetches each /q URL with JS disabled and asserts the H1, the verdict and the first-paragraph answer are in the raw HTML.

issues.where: sourcesHtml() in template.html: hard-coded 'Quote checked on the page, 18 Oct 2026'
issues.problem: The same check date is printed under every source on every page, drafts included. It is a template literal, not a recorded fact. A citation date that isn't the real per-quote check date breaks Hum's own honesty rule. If a fact-checker or Wikipedia editor relies on it and finds the quote has changed, Hum loses its credibility as a citation.
issues.fix: Store a checked date per source (the spec's 'retrieved' field) and render that. Leave the line out entirely when there is no date. Add a lint that fails the build on a source without a retrieved date.

issues.where: <head> of template.html; answer(), topic(), today() renderers
issues.problem: Every page has <title>Hum Answers prototype</title>. There is no meta description, canonical, Open Graph or Twitter card tag, and document.title never changes. Search results and link previews (WhatsApp, Slack, X) would all read 'Hum Answers prototype' with no answer in them. For a site whose growth depends on links being shared, this hurts most.
issues.fix: For each prerendered page, write <title>{H1} | Hum</title>, a meta description of '{Verdict}: {result}. {first sentence with numbers}' (at most 155 characters), a self-referencing canonical, and og:title/og:description/og:image. The OG image should be a generated card showing the verdict stamp and the range.

issues.where: Answer page first paragraph (screenshot: Google search myth); reviewed.json 'answer' fields
issues.problem: Answer engines quote the first one or two sentences under the H1. On the Google-search page, the first sentence is backstory ('The 10× came from the IEA's 2024 report…'), and the verdict is two badges (PARTLY, OUT OF DATE) with no sentence attached. A snippet would lift the history, not the answer. The 'result' field ('Out of date') doesn't work alone either.
issues.fix: Open every reviewed answer with one self-contained sentence that names the subject and states the verdict and the number. Example: 'Partly. The 10× figure is out of date: newer estimates put a short ChatGPT question at about 0.3 Wh, roughly the same as Google's last published 0.3 Wh per search (2009).' Put the backstory after it. Add a lint that requires a digit and the stamp word in sentence one.

issues.where: drafts.json (310 entries, ~299 shown) and the 'd-' slugs in template.html
issues.problem: If the 299 unreviewed drafts are published as indexable pages next to 11 reviewed ones, the site is mostly thin, unreviewed content. Search engines judge site quality as a whole, and AI engines will cite a draft verdict as if it were Hum's settled position. Several drafts also overlap reviewed pages, for example 'does asking chatgpt really use 10 times more energy than a google search?'. Slugs are cut off mid-phrase ('do-thinking-or-reasoning-modes-like-gpt-5-or').
issues.fix: Mark drafts noindex (meta robots and X-Robots-Tag) and leave them out of the sitemap until they are promoted. Redirect any draft that overlaps a reviewed answer (301 to /q/{reviewed-slug}). Generate slugs from a short hand-written H1, never by truncating the question, and freeze each slug at promotion.

issues.where: Answer pages (no structured data, no visible updated date)
issues.problem: Nothing machine-readable says this is a fact-check of a named claim, by whom, rated what, and when. There is no visible 'Updated' or 'Reviewed' date near the H1. Engines that weigh freshness can't tell a 2026 answer from a 2019 one, which matters on a page whose own verdict is 'out of date'.
issues.fix: Add JSON-LD to each reviewed /q page. Use ClaimReview (claimReviewed = the quoted claim, reviewRating with alternateName = YES/PARTLY/NO) on myth pages: Google Fact Check Explorer and other fact-check aggregators read it, even though Google no longer shows it as a rich result. Use Article (or QAPage) with datePublished/dateModified and publisher 'Hum' on the others. Show 'Reviewed {date} · version link' under the H1.

issues.where: Share box ('Copy to share') and the absence of Cite
issues.problem: The copied text drops the https:// scheme ('Sources: humearth.org/q/…'), so many apps won't turn it into a link. Journalists, teachers and Wikipedia editors (the spec's second audience) get no cite string, accessed date or versioned URL. Those are the people whose links give the site authority.
issues.fix: Use the full https:// canonical in the share text. Add the spec's Cite option (APA and {{cite web}} with the version URL /q/{slug}/v/{date}) under 'More' on reviewed pages now. It costs little and it is the main source of backlinks.

issues.where: Home H1 and topic/answer copy; the 'Prototype for testing' banner on every view
issues.problem: The home H1 never says 'data centres', and answer H1s use Hum's own wording ('thinking modes') rather than what people type ('reasoning models', 'o3', 'ChatGPT energy per query'). There are no alternative phrasings on the page. The prototype banner is the first text on every page, so a crawler would take it as the snippet.
issues.fix: Add an 'Also asked as' line with the bank's near-duplicate questions (that also uses the merged draft IDs well). Put 'data centres' in the home H1 or the line under it. Make the banner removable by a build flag so it never ships to production HTML.

keep: The question as the H1, then a one-word verdict stamp, then the plain answer: the right shape for featured snippets and AI Overviews.
The range bar with named low/mid/high sources (0.24 / 0.34 / 1.86 Wh) also written in the text, so engines quote a range instead of one number.
Verbatim source quotes, each with a provenance chip ('Company says so', 'Estimated'); the labelled company claims are what make Hum safer to cite than most explainers.
Showing 'Hum's sums' (77 Wh ÷ 0.34 Wh ≈ 230): the arithmetic I re-checked on five pages is correct, and showing it lets others verify and cite it.
The 'What nobody knows yet' fold: stating the gaps openly is good for trust and gives answer engines a quotable 'unknown'.
The world-total clause comparing consumption with consumption (485 TWh against France's 480.6 TWh demand).
The spec's plan of prerendered /q/{slug} pages that work without JS, versioned URLs and a robots.txt that welcomes AI search bots: build exactly that.
reviews.persona: an SEO and answer-engine specialist (Google, AI Overviews, chatbots citing sources) judging findability and citability

reviews.first_10_seconds: "Okay, it's a myth-buster for AI's energy, water and CO2, with a quiz card to tap. That's clear. The headline does its job, and I'd tap a guess because a four-option quiz is hard to resist. But I can't tell yet why I'd send this to anyone, or why I'd come back tomorrow."
reviews.verdict: The front door has finally fixed the "what is this?" problem. A one-line promise, a search box and a guess card are the right three things, and the guess-then-reveal pattern does keep people for the first minute. The growth loop is missing, though. Nothing here makes someone want to share it, and nothing brings them back. The first card's correct answer is factually wrong ("a few seconds of a phone charge" is really one to four minutes), and that card is the one everyone sees. The reveal also lands on a mushy headline, "Less than a phone charge", when the real shock line is "one fiftieth of a phone charge". "Today" on launch day shows the same card as the home page, numbered #142 as though 141 days came before it. That is a made-up history on a site whose whole pitch is honesty, and it repeats after 11 days. The share text is "Hum #142: missed it" plus a long question and a URL, with no number and no hook, so nobody would click it. Shared links have no preview: the title is "Hum Answers prototype", and there are no og tags or image. The answer pages carry real credibility capital, with verbatim quotes, "company says so" labels and the out-of-date stamp. That trust is the moat. Right now it's buried under folds and never turned into a shareable artifact. Fix the first card, give each reveal a stat line someone would screenshot, make Today a real daily ritual with honest numbering and a score, and this could spread. As it stands, people will nod, maybe play three cards, and leave.

issues.where: Home card 1 / Today card (reviewed.json, slug one-question, guess.options[0] and result)
issues.problem: The marked-correct answer, 'A few seconds of a phone charge', is wrong by about 10 to 100 times. The figures are 0.34 Wh against 19 Wh per charge, so about 1.8% of a charge. A phone charger draws roughly 5 to 20 W, so 0.34 Wh is about 1 to 4 minutes of charging, not seconds. This is the first fact every visitor sees, and anyone who checks it will distrust everything after it. The result line 'Less than a phone charge' also undersells the point: it would be true of something 50 times bigger.
issues.fix: Change the option to 'About 1/50 of a phone charge' (or 'A minute or two of phone charging', with the charger wattage stated and sourced). Change result to 'About 1/50 of a phone charge (roughly 10 to 80 questions per charge)'. Keep the other three distractors.

issues.where: Today page (template.html today(), n = 142 + day; PLAY rotation of 11)
issues.problem: On launch day, Today shows exactly the same card as the home page, so returning visitors get nothing new. '#142' invents 141 past puzzles that never existed, which is a fabricated detail on a site sold on honesty. With 11 cards, the 'daily' question repeats every 11 days. There's no streak and no tomorrow teaser, so there's no reason to come back.
issues.fix: Start numbering at #1 on the real launch date. Make the home card differ from Today's card, or make Today the only daily card. Add 'Tomorrow: <topic>' plus a local-only streak ('3 days in a row, kept on this device only', which fits the no-accounts rule). Don't launch Today until there are at least 30 reviewed playable cards, or label it 'Hum #1 of 11'.

issues.where: Today share text (template.html line 297) and answer share text (line 320)
issues.problem: The Today share text is 'Hum #142: missed it · "How much electricity does one ChatGPT question use?" · humearth.org/today'. It has no surprising number, no score visual and no curiosity gap, so it's worse than Wordle's grid. The answer-page share uses the answer's first sentence, which is often process, not punchline. For example: 'The claim traces to a UC Riverside study (Li et al.)' or 'Hugging Face's AI Energy Score team measured open models directly.' Nobody forwards those.
issues.fix: Add a hand-written 'shareLine' field to every reviewed answer. It should be a single sourced sentence with the number in it, e.g. 'ChatGPT doesn't drink a bottle of water per email. It's 10 to 50 answers per bottle. Sources: humearth.org/q/bottle-of-water'. For Today, use 'Hum #N ✓ / ✕ · I guessed X, the answer was Y · can you beat it? humearth.org/today' so the share opens a curiosity gap without giving the answer away.

issues.where: <head> of template.html
issues.problem: The title is 'Hum Answers prototype', and there's no description, no og:title and no og:image per answer. When people paste a link into WhatsApp, iMessage, X or LinkedIn, they get a bare URL, and link previews drive most clicks on shared links. The hash routes (#bottle-of-water) can't carry per-answer previews at all.
issues.fix: Give each reviewed answer a real path (/q/slug), prerendered at build time, with og:title set to the claim, og:description set to the verdict plus the number, and a generated 1200x630 card image: verdict stamp, the claim struck through or confirmed, the range bar and 'every number sourced'. That card image is the shareable artifact.

issues.where: Reveal 'The bigger picture' (every card's world field) and the home section also headed 'The bigger picture'
issues.problem: Every card ends on the same sentence ('485 TWh in 2025, more than France…'), so by card 3 it reads as boilerplate and people skip it. The section below the card uses the same heading for a list of questions, which is confusing. The world-share card says 415 TWh in 2024 while the reveal says 485 TWh in 2025. Both are correct, but showing them side by side looks like a contradiction to a casual reader.
issues.fix: Write a card-specific bigger-picture line for each card, e.g. bills leads to the PJM capacity price and water to total data-centre water. Show the France line once, on card 1 only. Rename the home list to 'Questions people ask'. On the world-share reveal, add 'rising to 485 TWh in 2025' so the two years connect.

issues.where: Answer page 'my-year' (reviewed.json answer text)
issues.problem: '18 billion messages a week from 700 million users, about 26 each' leaves out 'a week'. Readers will take it as 26 a year, and then the 0.46 kWh figure looks about 50 times too high. The arithmetic is right (26 × 52 × 0.34 Wh ≈ 0.46 kWh), but the sentence makes it look wrong.
issues.fix: Write 'about 26 each a week, or about 1,350 a year'.

issues.where: Range bar caption on claim answers (rangeText in template.html)
issues.problem: The claim note is appended as its own sentence, which produces a lowercase fragment: '...middle 0.34 (OpenAI). the 2.9 Wh behind "10×".' On a site that sells care, this looks sloppy.
issues.fix: Render it as '...middle 0.34 (OpenAI). The claim used 2.9 Wh.' Capitalize the note, or write the claim notes as full sentences.

issues.where: How big is that? ladder (video 90 Wh then kettle 99 Wh)
issues.problem: 'about 1× the rung above' is a dead rung that tells the reader nothing, and it breaks the drama of the step-up ladder right before the big jump.

The one-line promise, 'AI's electricity, water and CO2: straight answers, every number sourced.' Clear in under 10 seconds.
'Heard something? Ask Hum.' with a real claim as the example: it puts the visitor's own question first.
Verdict stamps (YES/PARTLY/NO/NOBODY KNOWS) and the 'OUT OF DATE' tag: instantly legible and screenshot-friendly.
'Company says so' and 'Estimated' labels with verbatim quotes and 'checked on the page': the trust moat no competitor has.
The 'What nobody knows yet' fold: honesty that makes the rest believable.
The 'How big is that?' log ladder from one question to all data centres: the best scale-sense device on the site.
Draft answers clearly boxed as unreviewed: keeps the 299-answer breadth without risking credibility.
No sign-up, no tracking, and the device-only tally.

reviews.first_10_seconds: Okay, it's a quiz about AI's electricity use with a search box on top. The first card tells me straight away what the game is: guess what one ChatGPT question costs. I'd tap an answer, so the hook works. Then I picked the obvious "smallest" option, it said I was right, and I realised three of the four choices were jokes. As a player I'd stop trusting the game after card two.
reviews.verdict:
The guess-then-reveal card is the right core mechanic for this site. It is the only thing on the front door that makes a stranger do something in the first 10 seconds, and handing off from the reveal to a fully sourced answer page is a real advantage. But the game is designed like a form, not a game.

1. **The flagship card is wrong.** Its "correct" option, "a few seconds of a phone charge", is both unsourced and off by about 30x.
2. **The distractors are too easy.** Most cards have one sensible option and three absurd ones, so players learn nothing about scale, which is the whole point.
3. **The reveal misleads visually.** It paints the player's wrong pick in solid amber and the right one in a faint outline.
4. **"Today" is not a daily game yet.** It reuses the 11-card home deck, so on day one it is the exact card already on the home screen. It repeats every 11 days and starts at a made-up #142.
5. **There is no end state and nothing worth bragging about.** The share line is just "got it" or "missed it".

Fix the phone-charge figure before anyone plays this. After that, the changes that would turn this into a loop people return to:
- Log-spaced options that all sound plausible.
- Scoring by how close the guess was.
- An end-of-run screen.
- A separate daily deck.
- A share line that shows how far off you were.

issues.where: Home card 1 / Today card, 'one-question' guess options (reviewed.py line 57); reveal headline 'Less than a phone charge'
issues.problem: The correct option says 0.34 Wh is 'a few seconds of a phone charge'. By Hum's own EPA figure (19 Wh per charge), 0.34 Wh is about 1.8% of a charge. At a typical 1.5 to 2 hour charge that is roughly 1.5 to 2 minutes, not seconds. No source gives a charging time, so 'seconds' is both unsourced and about 30x wrong. The reveal headline 'Less than a phone charge' then understates a roughly 50x gap. Players will repeat the headline card first, so it is the worst place for an error.
issues.fix: Change the option to 'About 1/50 of a phone charge' (0.34 ÷ 19 ≈ 0.018, add this to calc). Change the result to 'About a fiftieth of a phone charge'. Make every option a fraction or multiple of the 19 Wh EPA charge or the 99 Wh kettle so each one traces to the ladder. Drop the fridge unless it gets a sourced figure.

issues.where: Option design across how-much cards (one-question, my-year, world-share, power-mix)
issues.problem: The distractors don't test anything. For one-question the right answer is the only small option, against a phone charge, a kettle (300x) and a fridge-day. For my-year it is 0.2 kg against 20 kg, 2 tonnes and 'Nobody knows'. Players win by picking the modest-sounding option, so the 'wow' never lands. 'Nobody knows' as a decoy on a card that has a firm answer also cheapens the honest NOBODY KNOWS verdict used elsewhere.
issues.fix: Use four plausible, log-spaced options around the truth (for example 1/500, 1/50, 1/5 and 1 phone charge), so a wrong guess is wrong by 10x rather than by a joke. Better still, replace the buttons with a 'drag to guess' log slider over the ladder and score closeness ('you were 12x too high'). Keep 'Nobody knows' only on cards whose real answer is NOBODY KNOWS.

issues.where: Reveal state of the card (bindCard: chosen button aria-pressed vs .right class); screenshot after guessing 'Boiling a kettle'
issues.problem: The wrong guess the player picked ends up filled in solid amber, the brand's strongest and most 'correct-looking' style. The actual right answer only gets a thin white outline. At a glance it reads as if the kettle was correct.
issues.fix: Mark the right answer with a filled style and a check ('✓ Right answer'). Mark a wrong pick with a muted fill and '✕ Your guess', and dim the other two. Put the right answer's label in the reveal headline: 'Not quite. About 1/50 of a phone charge.'

issues.where: Today page (today() picks from PLAY, n = 142 + day)
issues.problem: The daily question is drawn from the same 11-card deck as the home page, in the same order. On launch day 'Today' is the exact card already on the home first screen. It repeats every 11 days, and '#142' on day one invents a history that doesn't exist, which fits badly with a site whose product is honesty. Nothing stops a replay after a refresh, so 'got it' is meaningless.
issues.fix: Use a separate dated daily deck (build it from the 299 drafts once they are reviewed, and start with at least 30). Number it from #1 on launch day. Store today's answer in localStorage so a revisit shows your result instead of a fresh card, and leave Today's card out of the home rotation.

issues.where: Home card loop: 11 progress dots, 'Next question', tally line
issues.problem: There is no end to a run. After card 11 it silently wraps to card 1. The tally counts every play, including replays and Today, so it inflates. A finished run gives no payoff and no prompt to share, so the loop has a start but no climax.
issues.fix: After the last dot, show an end card: 'You got 7 of 11. Your biggest miss: kettle, 300x too high.' Offer a copyable share line and 'Ask Hum something' (focus the search box). Count each card once per device.

issues.where: Today share text: `Hum #n: got it/missed it · “q” · humearth.org/today`
issues.problem: The share line carries no result anyone would want to brag about or answer. 'missed it' plus the question isn't a hook. Wordle-style sharing works because the result shows how you did without giving away the answer.
issues.fix: Share how close you were without the answer, for example 'Hum #3: I guessed 300x too high. Can you beat me? humearth.org/today'. On claim cards: 'Hum #3: I said False. Hum said PARTLY.' Keep it as plain text with no tracking parameters.

issues.where: Reveal range bar on one-question and google-search (bar lowNote 'Google (Gemini)', highNote 'large open model, MIT Technology Review', midNote 'OpenAI')
issues.problem: The first thing a player sees after guessing is a single axis with Gemini at the low end, OpenAI in the middle and an open model at the top. That reads as a ranking of AI models measured in different ways, which breaks a fixed Hum rule. The 0.24 and 1.86 labels are also about 7px on a phone and can't be read.
issues.fix: Label the bar 'Published estimates, measured different ways' and drop company names from the end labels: show them in the sources fold, not on the bar. Raise the SVG label size so they are at least 12px at a 375px width.

issues.where: Reveal 'The bigger picture' callout plus the home section of the same name; world clause on 8 of 11 cards
issues.problem: The reveal's payoff line is the same 485 TWh / France sentence on 8 of 11 cards, so from card 3 on the reward is a rerun. Directly below, a section also called 'The bigger picture' lists unrelated YES/PARTLY questions, and the reused name muddles both. The Today screenshot also shows 'A day of a fridge' highlighted before any tap, which looks preselected.
issues.fix: Give each card its own 'so what' line that ties its number to the total (for example 'all those questions add up to X% of data centres' use'), and save the 485 TWh line for the world-share card. Rename the home section 'Questions people argue about'. Clear the hover/focus style on load.

keep: Guess first, then reveal. Making the visitor commit before seeing the number is the only thing that turns the front door into an action, and it explains the site faster than the tagline does.
The 'Just tell me' escape hatch, which respects people who don't want to play.
The claim cards ('You've probably heard...') with a verdict stamp. Guessing true, partly or false on a viral claim is a strong, shareable format.
The range bar showing the claim marker against the sourced range on the bottle-of-water card: the 500 ml claim sits far outside the 10 to 50 ml band. That is the best reveal visual in the prototype.
'Read the full answer' straight from the reveal. The hand-off from game to sourced proof is Hum's edge over any trivia app.
No sign-up, no tracking, and a tally kept only on the device.
The 11-dot progress strip, which shows the run is short and finite (it just needs an end screen).

reviews.first_10_seconds: A site that answers AI-energy claims with sourced numbers, and lets me guess first. The playable card is a good hook. Then I look at the first range bar and can't tell what scale I'm on or what kind of range it is. For a site that sells itself on honesty, that is the wrong first chart.
reviews.verdict:
The prose is careful: it hedges by provenance, prints the calculations, quotes the sources and is open about what nobody knows. The graphics undo that work.

The range bar is on an unlabelled log scale whose domain floats with each page (min/2.2 to max×2.2). It has no ticks and no zero. The band it draws is not an uncertainty interval. It is the spread between three different models measured three different ways, and the one company figure in the middle is labelled "middle".

The ladder draws log-scale bars from an arbitrary 0.1 Wh floor, so people will read bar length as quantity. Its multipliers are point-estimate integers, which produce "about 1×" and, on the world-share page, "about 17,321,428,571× the rung above".

The very first card's correct answer, "a few seconds of a phone charge", is off by more than an order of magnitude by Hum's own figures.

I would not share this until the scale, the meaning of the band and that arithmetic are fixed. All of them can be fixed. The data and the quotes underneath are good enough to deserve better charts.

issues.where: Home playable card, one-question guess (reviewed.py line 57: options[0], right=0)
issues.problem: The correct answer is 'A few seconds of a phone charge'. By Hum's own figures, 0.34 Wh ÷ 19 Wh is about 1.8% of a charge. The EPA figure assumes roughly 2 hours of charging, so that is about 2 minutes, not seconds. At the published high of 1.86 Wh it is about 10%, or around 12 minutes. The keyed answer understates the energy 20 to 200 times, and no sourced charging time or wattage supports 'seconds'. Hum's first impression teaches a wrong fact.
issues.fix: Make the option 'About 2% of a phone charge' and the reveal 'About 1 to 10% of one phone charge (0.24 to 1.86 Wh ÷ 19 Wh)'. Add that calculation to calc[]. If you want a time unit, source a charging wattage first.

issues.where: Answer page ladder fold, last rung (template.html ladderHtml; shown on world-share)
issues.problem: The step from 'A US home for a day' (28,000 Wh) to 'All the world's data centres' (485 TWh) renders as 'about 17,321,428,571× the rung above'. That is an 11-significant-figure multiplier built from two rounded estimates, and nobody can read it. The spec also requires a town-year rung and an 'AI's share of data centres' rung; both are missing, so the ladder jumps 10 orders of magnitude in one step.
issues.fix: Add the spec's missing rungs (town-year, AI's share of data centres with its range), so no step is bigger than about 1,000×. Format multipliers to 1–2 significant figures with words: 'about 17 billion ×'.

issues.where: Range bar on the card and answer pages (rangeSvg, template.html line 172)
issues.problem: The scale is log10, but the chart doesn't say so and has no ticks, gridlines or zero. Its domain floats per page (min/2.2 to max×2.2), so the same band looks a different size on each chart. Readers read it as linear: OpenAI's 0.34 sits about 17% along the 0.24–1.86 band, where on a linear scale it would be about 6%. On the water page the log scale shrinks the 10× gap between 50 ml and the 500 ml claim into a modest distance, which visually weakens the debunk.
issues.fix: Use a linear axis from 0 whenever the range plus the claim span less than about 50× (true of every bar today: 0 to 2.9 Wh, 0 to 500 ml). That makes the myth's distance visible. If you keep log for wider spans, draw labelled decade ticks (0.1, 1, 10) and write 'log scale' on the axis. Fix the domain per quantity, not per page.

issues.where: Range bar band + caption: 'from 0.24 (Google (Gemini)) to 1.86 (large open model…), middle 0.34 (OpenAI)'
issues.problem: The band is not uncertainty about one quantity. It puts three models on one axis, each measured a different way: Google's median prompt (company, wide boundary), OpenAI's 'average query' (company, undisclosed boundary) and an MIT TR estimate for Llama 3.1 405B (GPU energy doubled). Placing them left to right by name ranks models across boundaries, which Hum's rules forbid. It also mixes a median with a mean. 'Middle' implies a central estimate, but 0.34 is not the middle (the geometric middle is about 0.67). Both company figures carry no company label on the chart. The dashed band is DESIGN.md's style for an uncertainty range, so the chart claims more than the data supports.
issues.fix: Caption the band 'Spread of published figures (different models, measured different ways)', not 'from…to'. Rename 'middle' to 'OpenAI says' and draw it as a hollow company-claim marker rather than the solid amber central value. Put a boundary chip on each end, or drop the model names from the ends and list them in the sources.

issues.where: Ladder bars (ladderHtml: log10 from 0.1 Wh to 1e15 Wh, filled from 0)
issues.problem: Log-scale bars filled from an arbitrary floor are a known misreading trap: bar length reads as quantity. The phone charge (19 Wh) bar is about 1/7 of the track and a US home-day (28 kWh) about 1/3, so it looks like a home uses about 2.5 phone charges a day instead of about 1,500. The only warning sits in a footnote under the whole list and says 'each step is ten times bigger', but there are no steps drawn.
issues.fix: Replace the bars with dots on one shared log axis. Label decade ticks along the top (1 Wh, 1 kWh, 1 MWh … 1 TWh) and connect the dots, so position, not length, carries the value. Or drop the graphic and let the 'N× the rung above' text twin do the work. Put the 'log scale' note above the ladder, not below it.

issues.where: Ladder multipliers 'about N× the rung above'
issues.problem: Integer rounding gives 'about 1× the rung above' for kettle vs AI video (99/90 = 1.1), which says nothing. Every multiplier also uses point estimates even when a rung has a range: the first rung's own note says 0.24 to 1.86 Wh, so 'about 56×' is really 10× to 80×. Showing a single multiplier off a ranged rung is false precision.
issues.fix: Use 'about the same' under 1.5×, 1 decimal place under 10×, and 2 significant figures above that. Wherever a rung carries a range, print the multiplier as a range ('10 to 80× the rung above'), as the answer text already does for phone charges.

issues.where: Ladder provenance and styling (reviewed.json ladder 'kind'; all fills solid)
issues.problem: The kettle rung is Hum's own physics sum (a lower bound) but is tagged kind 'Measured'. The US home rung is an Epoch AI average and is also tagged 'Measured'. Every rung is drawn as the same solid fill. DESIGN.md requires calculated values to be dashed or hatched, and the spec requires a boundary chip on every rung. Nothing in the visual separates measured, estimated, company and calculated rungs.
issues.fix: Retag the kettle as 'Calculated (lower bound)' and the home as 'Estimated'. Hatch the calculated rung and draw the lower bound as an open-ended arrow. Give the company rung (0.34 Wh) the company marker, and add the boundary chip per rung the spec calls for.

issues.where: 'The bigger picture' on 9 of 11 answers: '485 TWh in 2025, more than France (481 TWh)'
issues.problem: 'More than' asserts an order from a 4 TWh (0.8%) gap between an IEA estimate, which has a wide uncertainty and its own scenario range, and an Ember demand figure. The data can't tell those two apart. The same sentence is pasted onto Netflix, flights, reasoning and power mix, where it is not the relevant scale.
issues.fix: Say 'about as much as France uses in a year (Ember: 481 TWh of demand)' and keep 'consumption' explicit for both. Write a world clause that fits each answer, or leave it out.

keep: The guess-then-reveal card. Asking for a guess before showing the number is one of the few things that reliably fixes people's misjudged magnitudes.
Printing the claim's own number on the same axis as the evidence (2.9 Wh behind '10×', the 500 ml claim). It is the right encoding for a myth check; it just needs a linear scale so the gap shows.
The text twin under every chart (the rangeText caption doubling as aria-label). Readers who can't parse the graphic still get low, high and who said it.
The published calc[] lines ('19 Wh ÷ 1.86 Wh ≈ 10') and the hedge-by-provenance labels (Company says so, Estimated) on the sources. The ladder and range bar should copy these.
The 'What nobody knows yet' fold. Naming the missing measurement (OpenAI's undisclosed boundary, Google's search figure) is better uncertainty communication than any band.
The ladder concept itself: one question to all data centres, with this answer's rung highlighted. Fix the scale and the multipliers, don't cut it.
reviews.persona: a data-visualisation and uncertainty-communication scientist judging the range bars and the ladder

reviews.first_10_seconds: "A fact-check site for AI's energy use, and it wants me to play a guessing game. Okay, I get it: rumours about ChatGPT and electricity get checked here. But the headline is a list of nouns plus a promise about method, 'every number sourced'. It doesn't tell me why I should care. The line that would have hooked me, that all the data centres together use about as much power as France, is hidden until after I guess."
reviews.verdict: This version understands its job much better than the current site. "Heard something? Ask Hum." is a real promise in five words, the guess card gives a cold visitor something to do in the first second, and the answer pages sound honest and plain instead of preachy. But the brand rests on precision, and the first thing a visitor touches is wrong. The correct answer on the opening card says one question is "a few seconds of a phone charge". By Hum's own figures (0.34 Wh against 19 Wh a charge) it is about 2% of a charge, which is a minute or two of charging, not seconds. The signature line also says "more than France" when the two numbers are 485 and 481 TWh. They are less than 1% apart, and the estimates and their definitions (IEA consumption against Ember demand) are not that exact. A sceptic who checks either one stops trusting the rest. Beyond that, the voice slips in the places that decide whether people share: the share texts carry no fact, "The bigger picture" names four different things, and the 10× page shows two stamps (PARTLY and OUT OF DATE) that disagree with each other. Fix the card's arithmetic, soften France to "about as much as", rewrite the share lines around the surprising fact, and this is a voice people would quote. As it stands I'd play one card and leave, and I wouldn't forward it, because the share text gives me nothing worth sending.

issues.where: Home and Today guess card, 'one-question' (reviewed.py line 57, option 0 and result)
issues.problem: The marked-correct option, 'A few seconds of a phone charge', is factually wrong. 0.34 Wh ÷ 19 Wh is about 1.8% of a charge, roughly 1 to 2 minutes of charging. Even the low Gemini figure (0.24 Wh) is about 1.3%. The reveal headline 'Not quite. Less than a phone charge.' also doesn't match the option's wording, so a visitor can't tell which option was right. The sentence that makes the answer land ('One phone charge is roughly 10 to 80 short questions') is cut off by firstSentence() in the reveal.
issues.fix: Change option 0 to 'About 1/50th of a phone charge', or use the quote Hum already has from Altman: 'about what an oven uses in a little over one second'. Set result to 'About 1/50th of a phone charge'. Make the reveal read 'You got it. About 1/50th of a phone charge: one charge is 10 to 80 short questions.' Show the answer's first two sentences plus the per-charge line, not just the first sentence.

issues.where: WORLD clause (reviewed.py line 51), shown in every card reveal and on 9 answer pages
issues.problem: '485 TWh in 2025, more than France (481 TWh)' turns a gap of less than 1% between an IEA estimate (consumption) and Ember's measured demand into a ranking. For a brand whose whole promise is 'a verdict can't be stronger than its evidence', the signature line overclaims.
issues.fix: 'All the world's data centres used about 485 TWh in 2025, about as much electricity as France uses in a year, and the IEA expects that to roughly double by 2030.' Do the same in the world-share answer ('more than all of France uses' becomes 'about as much as France').

issues.where: Home headline (template.html line 274)
issues.problem: 'AI's electricity, water and CO2: straight answers, every number sourced.' is a category label plus a promise about method. It names no tension and no stakes, so it is the same 'what is this for?' problem the founder is trying to fix. The product's real hook (your question is tiny, the total is a country) appears only after a guess. 'CO2' also reads as unfinished; use CO₂.
issues.fix: Lead with the paradox: 'One AI question is tiny. All of them together use as much electricity as France. Hum gives you straight, sourced answers about both.' Keep 'Heard something? Ask Hum.' directly under it. Use CO₂ in all display text.

issues.where: 'The bigger picture' label (template.html lines 233, 279, 318, 327)
issues.problem: One phrase names four things: the world-total callout in the reveal, the home list of questions, the 'next questions' slot, and the world line on answer pages. On the home screen the callout labelled 'The bigger picture' sits right above a section headed 'The bigger picture' that is a list of unrelated questions. The label stops meaning anything.
issues.fix: Keep 'The bigger picture' only for the world-total line. Rename the home list 'What people ask Hum' or 'Start here'. Rename the next-question slot labels 'Go deeper', 'Zoom out' and 'Closer to home'.

issues.where: Answer page 'google-search' stamps, and the home list's stamp column
issues.problem: The 10× page shows two stamps, PARTLY and OUT OF DATE, while the body text concludes 'roughly similar, not proven'. Hum's own rule says PARTLY means 'the published range overlaps the claim', yet 2.9 Wh sits outside the 0.24 to 1.86 bar. On the home list the stamp column mixes verdicts (✓ YES, ◐ PARTLY) with a sentence in monospace caps ('Coal, at about 30%'), so the column has no consistent meaning.
issues.fix: Give each page one verdict. For the 10× page use OUT OF DATE as the verdict (or NOBODY KNOWS), with the result line 'Old numbers. Today a question and a search are probably similar.' Remove the second stamp. On the home list, show stamps only for claim pages and put the number answers ('About 30% coal') in the subline, not the stamp column.

issues.where: Share copy: Today (template.html line 297) and answer pages (line 320)
issues.problem: The Today share text, 'Hum #142: missed it · “One short ChatGPT question uses about as much electricity as…” · humearth.org/today', carries no fact and ends on a cliffhanger nobody will click. 'missed it' shames the sender. The answer share opens with 'Hum's answer: PARTLY. Out of date.', which is stamp jargon in caps. 'Would you send this?' is the founder's own test question, and this copy fails it. Today also repeats home card #1, and '#142' is a made-up count.
issues.fix: Share the surprise, not the score: 'One ChatGPT question ≈ 1/50th of a phone charge. All the world's data centres ≈ France. Sources: humearth.org/q/one-question'. Make the answer share read '“ChatGPT uses 10× a Google search”? Out of date: those were 2009 and 2024 numbers. humearth.org/q/google-search'. Make Today a different card from the home card, and number it from launch day.

issues.where: Range bar captions and ladder (template.html line 199; screenshots of the reveal and the answer page)
issues.problem: The copy has visible glitches: 'from 0.24 (Google (Gemini))' has a double parenthesis; '…middle 0.34 (OpenAI). the 2.9 Wh behind “10×”.' is a lowercase fragment; the ladder's 'about 1× the rung above' (90 Wh to 99 Wh) reads as a non-statement; 'rung' is jargon for a teenager; the card says 'Boiling a kettle' while the ladder says 'Boiling 1 litre of water'.
issues.fix: Write captions as one sentence: 'Published figures: 0.24 Wh (Google, Gemini) to 1.86 Wh (a large open model). OpenAI says 0.34. The dotted line is the old 2.9 Wh behind “10×”.' Use 'about the same as above' when the ratio is under 1.5, and replace 'the rung above' with 'than the line above'. Use 'Boiling a litre of water' everywhere.

issues.where: Topic page subline (template.html line 357) and the 'heard' attributions in reviewed.py
issues.problem: 'drafts by how often people ask' suggests Hum measures visitor demand, but Hum has no tracking. Unsourced attributions such as 'a common worry in comment threads' on the Netflix claim risk looking like straw men on a site that sources everything.
issues.fix: Use 'Reviewed answers first, then drafts.' and state the real sort order if there is one. For each 'heard' line, either link one real instance of the claim or say 'a claim we've seen repeated' without implying a count.

keep: "Heard something? Ask Hum." is the best line on the site: a promise and a call to action in five words.
"Guess first" and "Just tell me": playful without being cute, and they respect a visitor in a hurry.
"What nobody knows yet" as a named section. It is the brand's most distinctive honesty move.
One-line 'Why the claim misleads' explanations such as "A bottle per 10 to 50 answers became a bottle per answer as it was retold." These are quotable and fair.
Plain source labels: 'Company says so', 'Estimated', 'Quote checked on the page' with a date, and the dashed 'Draft answer… may change' banner.
Pairing every 'your use is tiny' answer with the world total, so the site never reads as either a reassurance machine or a guilt machine.
The 'How big is that?' ladder from one question up to all data centres, once the wording is fixed.
Admitting what it hasn't checked: 'Hum read these figures in trade-press reports… still need checking on the page.'

reviews.first_10_seconds: A myth-buster for AI energy claims, with a pub-quiz card stuck on the front. "Every number sourced" is a big promise, so let me check the first number. The right answer to the first card is "a few seconds of a phone charge". 0.34 Wh out of 19 Wh is 1.8% of a charge. On any normal charger that's one to two minutes, not a few seconds. So the opening question already gets the arithmetic wrong.
reviews.verdict: The sourcing is better than 95% of what gets posted on this topic. Verbatim quotes, the date each was checked, "Company says so" labels and visible working all earn real credit, and most of the arithmetic holds up when I redo it. 77/0.34 is about 226. 246 kg / 0.16 g is about 1.5M. 18e9/7e8 × 52 × 0.34 Wh is about 0.45 kWh, and that times 473 g is about 0.22 kg. 6,706 J / 3,600 is 1.86 Wh. 0.000085 gal × 3,785 is 0.32 ml. 85 kcal × 4.184 is about 99 Wh. The problems are in the words around the numbers, and those are the parts a reader shares. The front-door answer ("a few seconds of a phone charge") is off by about 30×. One reviewed page says thinking modes cost "10 to 100×", while another says 150–700×. The water page stamps NO by blaming the claim on a 2023 GPT-3 paper. It also sets aside the 2024 GPT-4 "bottle per email" figure, which is where the meme actually came from and which supports it. The headline "more than France" rests on a 0.9% gap between two figures defined differently. The range bar puts Google's median, OpenAI's undefined average and MIT's Llama-405B estimate on one axis as low, middle and high, which breaks Hum's own rule against ranking across measurement boundaries. The "nobody knows" fold on the 10× page says the IEA's 2.9 Wh has no method, but Hum's own draft bank traces it to de Vries 2023. On HN, the top comment would be one of these, and after that nobody trusts the other 300 pages. Fix the verdict prose before any user test. The infrastructure is fine.

issues.where: Home and Today card (q002 guess) and its reveal
issues.problem: The correct option is "A few seconds of a phone charge". 0.34 Wh ÷ 19 Wh is 1.8% of a charge. On a typical 10–20 W charger, putting 0.34 Wh into the phone takes about 1–2 minutes, and at the 1.86 Wh high end it's about 5–10 minutes. Even on a fast charger it's 30–60 s, not a few seconds. The reveal ("Not quite. Less than a phone charge.") never gives the fraction, so the error goes unnoticed. It's also the first fact every visitor sees.
issues.fix: Change the option to "About 2% of a phone charge" (or "A minute or two of charging"). Have the reveal state the sum: "0.34 ÷ 19 ≈ 1.8%, so about 55 short questions per charge (10–80 across published figures)". Add that line to calc.

issues.where: q002 one-question answer: "Pasting in a long document or using a thinking mode can use 10 to 100 times more"
issues.problem: Nothing sourced supports this for thinking modes. The reasoning page (q006), citing Hugging Face, says 30× on average and 150–700× for the same model with reasoning on, so the two reviewed pages contradict each other. For long documents, the cited Epoch figures are 2.5 Wh (2.5/0.34 ≈ 7×) and 40 Wh (≈ 118×). That's roughly 7–120×, not 10–100×, and it describes long input, not thinking mode.
issues.fix: Split the sentence. Long documents: "about 7× (10k-token input) to over 100× (100k tokens), per Epoch AI". Thinking modes: "30× on average across open models, up to 150–700× for the same model, per Hugging Face; no figures for ChatGPT". Put both sums in calc. Add a build check that flags multipliers stated differently on different pages.

issues.where: q003 bottle-of-water, stamp NO
issues.problem: The viral claim ("a bottle of water per email") comes from the 2024 reporting by the same UC Riverside team: about 519 ml for a 100-word GPT-4 email. That supports the claim. The page swaps in the 2023 GPT-3 paper (10–50 answers per bottle) as the origin, mentions the GPT-4 figure only in "what nobody knows", sets it aside as unreadable, and stamps NO anyway. Leaving out the evidence that cuts against your verdict is a debunk of a strawman. "Most of it evaporated at the power stations" has no supporting quote. It also compares Li's scope-1+2 water with company figures that may be scope-1 only, as the page half-admits.
issues.fix: Change the stamp to NOBODY KNOWS (or PARTLY: "for GPT-4 in some US states, one team's model said roughly yes; companies now say about 0.3 ml"). Get the WaPo/UCR figure checked on the page, or say the verdict can't be given until it is. Remove "most of it evaporated at the power stations" unless a quote supports it.

issues.where: WORLD clause on almost every page, bigger-picture box, q026
issues.problem: "485 TWh, more than France (481 TWh)" is a 0.9% gap. That's far inside any uncertainty in an IEA estimate, and it compares IEA data-centre consumption with Ember's national demand (generation plus net imports, including losses). Two different definitions, and CLAUDE.md says to state consumption vs generation explicitly. The France "quote" is also Hum's own paraphrase ("France, 2025, electricity demand: 480.6 TWh (row checked…)"), shown in quotation marks with "Quote checked on the page". q026 also mixes editions: it puts 415 TWh (2024, Energy and AI 2025) next to 485 TWh (2025, Key Questions 2026), which implies 17% growth across a possible revision.
issues.fix: Say "about as much electricity as France uses in a year". Label it "consumption" and note that Ember's figure is national demand. Show the dataset row as a data citation (file, row, sha256), not as a blockquote. Take 2024 and 2025 from the same IEA edition, or say they come from different editions.

issues.where: Range bar on q002/q001 (Google 0.24 low, OpenAI 0.34 middle, MIT 1.86 high)
issues.problem: The bar ranks three numbers measured three ways on one axis. Google's is a median that counts idle capacity, host and cooling. OpenAI's is an "average" with no stated boundary. MIT's is one estimate for a single 405B open model. Calling OpenAI's figure the "middle" makes it look like a central estimate, which it isn't. This breaks Hum's fixed rule against ranking models across measurement boundaries, and the labels "Google (Gemini)" vs "large open model" read as a league table.

issues.where: q001 Google-search page, "What nobody knows yet": "The IEA didn't publish how it got 2.9 Wh"

The verdict is also fuzzy: the stamp says PARTLY, the chip says OUT OF DATE, and the text says "roughly similar, not proven". Those are three different verdicts.

The page's own unknowns say "Neither company separates AI from its other data-centre work", so YES contradicts its own unknowns. "Both point to building and running more data centres" and "Both still say they'll reach net zero (Google) or carbon negative (Microsoft) by 2030" have no supporting quote. The cited ESG Dive quote also says scope 2 fell 3%, and the answer leaves that out. The Microsoft quote has no subject (what rose 25%?), and every figure is secondhand from trade press.

OWID's travel factors are CO2-equivalent (for flights, UK factors include non-CO2 effects), compared here with CO2-only grid intensity. q004 says "typical user" but divides by weekly actives (a mean, not a typical user), counts messages as questions, and relies on an unsourced population (8.0–8.2bn).
