reviews.first_10_seconds: It's a myth-busting site about AI's electricity, water and CO2 that says every number is sourced. The quiz card is clever. Then the first answer I get is wrong in our favour, which worries me more than if it were wrong against us. Every page ends with the same line: "more than France, set to double". That is the line our critics use. I'll be reading this with a red pen, but it isn't a hit piece.
reviews.verdict: This is more even-handed than most of what lands on my desk. It says the 10x search myth is out of date, calls the bottle-per-email claim a NO, puts a year of ChatGPT at 0.2 kg of CO2, and labels company claims as company claims. I'd point journalists to several of these pages. But the framing still tilts. The one line repeated on every page is the most alarming one available: "485 TWh, more than France, roughly double by 2030". It shows no share of world demand, no IEA range and no growth context. "More than France" rests on a 4 TWh gap, under 1%, inside the IEA's own uncertainty. The big-tech emissions page answers YES to "because of AI" while its own fold admits neither company separates AI. It also drops the scope 2 figure the source quotes. The bills page uses only the PJM market monitor, read through trade press, and that monitor's counterfactual is contested. The range bar puts Google, OpenAI and an MIT estimate for a 405B open model on one scale, which breaks Hum's own rule against ranking across measurement boundaries. The first card has a plain arithmetic error: "a few seconds of a phone charge" is off by more than tenfold. I wouldn't share it until the arithmetic and the France line are fixed. After that I'd send it to reporters before most of what they read.

issues.where: Front door and Today guess card (q002 guess.options[0], the 'right' answer); reveal headline 'Less than a phone charge'
issues.problem: The correct option says one question uses about 'a few seconds of a phone charge'. The page's own numbers say 0.34 Wh against 19 Wh per charge, which is about 1/56 of a charge. A charge takes about 1.5 to 2 hours, so 1/56 of it is roughly 1.5 to 2 minutes, not seconds. That understates by 10 to 40 times. The reveal headline, 'Less than a phone charge', is so vague it says almost nothing. This is the first fact every visitor sees, and it is an arithmetic error that happens to favour AI. A critic will screenshot it and use it to cast doubt on the whole site.
issues.fix: Put the answer in energy, not time: 'About 1/50th of a phone charge'. Make the reveal match the answer text: 'About 1/50th of a phone charge: 10 to 80 short questions per charge, depending on whose figure you use.' Add the 19 ÷ 0.34 ≈ 56 sum to calc[], and add a check to build:data that every guess option agrees with the answer's own figures.

issues.where: 'The bigger picture' line, repeated on almost every reviewed answer and the front-door reveal: '485 TWh in 2025, more than France (481 TWh)'
issues.problem: This puts an IEA modelled estimate (485, 'roughly') against Ember's measured French demand (480.6) and states 'more than' on a gap under 1%. The IEA's own range for data centres is far wider than 4 TWh. The comparison claims a precision the sources don't have, and it is the same headline on every page.
issues.fix: Say 'about as much electricity as France uses in a year'. Add the share ('about 1.5% of world electricity in 2024, IEA') to the same line, so the scale comes with its denominator.

issues.where: Big tech emissions answer (q023), stamp YES, 'because of AI'

The answer also drops the sourced quote that Google's scope 2 emissions fell 3% while its electricity use rose 37%. It also relies only on trade-press reports of the primary documents, which breaks Hum's own rule that quotes are checked on the original page.

Check the quotes against Google's and Microsoft's own report PDFs before the page counts as reviewed, or label it Draft until then.

issues.where: Bills answer (q043) and the 'Your bills and the grid' shelf (24 questions, almost all drafts)
issues.problem: The reviewed answer rests on one source: PJM's market monitor, read through Utility Dive. That monitor's $7.3 billion 'data-centre-driven' figure is a disputed counterfactual, and the page doesn't mention that PJM, utilities and other analysts disagree. Nothing covers large-load tariffs, where data centres pay their own grid costs, or the national studies on whether load growth raises or spreads retail rates. The shelf's question titles repeat the framing ('pushing bills up' three times), and the drafts quote consumer advocates without matching voices.
issues.fix: Add at least one sourced counterpoint, checked on the page: for example Lawrence Berkeley National Lab or Brattle work on load growth and retail prices, and an example of a large-load tariff such as AEP Ohio's (already in your drafts). Label the $7.3 billion as 'the monitor's counterfactual estimate'. Reword the shelf titles neutrally, for example 'How do data centres affect electricity bills?'

issues.where: Range bar on the one-question and google-search pages: '0.24 (Google (Gemini)) ... middle 0.34 (OpenAI) ... 1.86 (large open model)'
issues.problem: This breaks Hum's own rule against ranking AI models measured in different ways. Google's 0.24 is a full-stack median that includes idle capacity and cooling overhead. OpenAI's 0.34 has no published method. MIT Technology Review's 1.86 is an estimate for Llama 3.1 405B, made by doubling GPU energy, and no consumer chatbot is known to run that model. Putting them on one scale with vendor names at low, middle and high reads as a league table. Labelling 1.86 'today' overstates what a typical question uses.
issues.fix: Remove vendor names from the bar ends, or show each figure as a separate dot with a 'measured differently' chip. Retitle the bar 'Published estimates (methods differ, not comparable)'. Footnote the 1.86 as 'a 405B open model, estimated by journalists, not a deployed chatbot'.

issues.where: 'The IEA expects that to roughly double by 2030', on every page
issues.problem: The IEA publishes scenario ranges. Your own draft on why forecasts disagree cites 'High Efficiency' around 700 TWh and 'Lift-Off' above 1,700 TWh for 2035. The headline gives only the base case and presents it as an expectation, and no page says that data centres are a small part of global demand growth next to industry, EVs and air conditioning. Without either, every page reads as alarm.
issues.fix: Write 'in its base case (its other scenarios run from X to Y)'. Add an IEA-sourced line, checked on the page, on data centres' share of global electricity demand growth to 2030, in the world-share answer and the 'How big is that?' ladder.

issues.where: Power-mix guess card (q029), 'Which source supplies the most… Coal'
issues.problem: This is a gotcha with no geography. The 30% coal figure is a global average pulled up by China's grid. A US or EU reader will take it as describing their local data centres. The answer explains location-based versus contracted power, which is good, but the card and the 'Coal, at about 30%' shelf label don't.
issues.fix: Add one sourced regional line to the reveal, for example the share of data-centre demand in China versus the US and what powers each. Rename the shelf label to 'Coal, about 30% worldwide (most from China's grid)'.

issues.where: Bottle-of-water answer (q003) 'Why the claim misleads'; ladder 'about 1× the rung above'; draft text
issues.problem: The 'per email' wording most likely comes from the 2024 Washington Post figure, which the page excludes because it couldn't be read. Blaming the inflation on 'retelling' of Li et al. may be the wrong origin, and an activist can rebut it in one tweet, which makes the NO look like industry spin. Two smaller problems: the ladder shows 'about 1×' between 90 Wh and 99 Wh, and some drafts slip into first person ('in the passages I read').
issues.fix: Say the email version comes from a newspaper estimate Hum couldn't verify, rather than claiming it came from retelling. Show the ladder multiplier to one decimal place, or hide it when the ratio is under 1.5. Strip first person from drafts in the generator.

keep: The 'Company says so' / 'Estimated' / 'Measured' chips on every source. They let me separate our members' claims from independent work, and keep you honest in both directions.

The google-search page. It traces the 10x claim to a 2009 Google figure set against an unexplained IEA 2.9 Wh, and ends at 'roughly similar, not proven'. That is fair and better sourced than most press coverage.
The 'What nobody knows yet' folds. Saying OpenAI hasn't published its method and nobody publishes a figure for thinking modes is the right kind of pressure, and it isn't spin.
Saying location-based versus contracted ('on paper') power outright on the power-mix page.
The year-of-use answer: about 0.2 kg of CO2 a year next to about 4.7 t per person, with the sums shown in calc. Proportion with working is exactly right.
Splitting water into direct use and power-plant use (17 billion versus 211 billion gallons, Berkeley Lab), and saying water is felt locally rather than globally.
Verbatim quotes, each marked as checked on the page, and the visible Draft label with its dashed box. Don't let draft answers lose that label.
The guess-then-reveal card as the front door. It gets people to engage before they make up their minds.

Make the search placeholder region-neutral, or give the bills shelf a first line ('evidence so far is mostly US and Ireland'). List other countries as 'nobody has published this yet' where true.
changes.why: Readers from India, the UK and Brazil all found the ladder, the bills shelf and the 'my bill' placeholder irrelevant to them.

changes.change: Share flow. Put a Share button on every reveal and answer, using navigator.share with a copy fallback, and hide the textarea. Add a hand-written sourced shareLine per answer with the number in it. Use full https:// URLs. Make the Today share line show the result without the answer. Add 'Cite this number' (primary source first, Hum URL, checked date).
changes.why: Testers had nothing worth forwarding. Verified: the share texts are generic and the URLs have no scheme.

changes.change: Search and draft handling. Rank reviewed answers first, and show '11 reviewed, 299 drafts'. On draft pages, put the one-line answer in the verdict-block layout and fold the body under 'Read the detail'. Mark drafts noindex until they are promoted.
changes.why: Drafts make up 96% of what search surfaces and read as dense blog text.

changes.change: Single-page-app accessibility. Set document.title for each view. Focus the h1 (not main) on route change. Make 'Next question' re-render only #card and focus the new prompt, which should be an h2. Give the search input a border of at least 3:1. Mark the stamp icons aria-hidden. Add html lang, and scroll-padding-top for the sticky header.
changes.why: Checked in the template: the title is static and Next re-renders the whole home view. Screen-reader users never hear the new question.

changes.change: For production, not this test: inline only the card deck and a compact search index, and fetch draft bodies when opened. Prerender /q/{slug}, /topics and /today as static HTML with a title, description and og:image for each, as the spec says. Self-host subset fonts instead of Google Fonts.
changes.why: Verified: the HTML is 818 KB, with 755 KB of drafts inlined. That is more than twice the 90 KB budget. Hash routes have no link previews, and the share URLs /q/slug aren't served. Google Fonts sends visitor IPs to Google.

changes.change: Write a one-sentence answer-first opening on each reviewed page (verdict word plus number). Add a rating guide linked from each stamp that defines YES, PARTLY, NO, NOBODY KNOWS and OUT OF DATE. Use 'CO₂' in display text. Use 'Boiling a litre of water' on both the card and the ladder. Change the topic subline 'by how often people ask' unless that is measured.
changes.why: Snippets and readers take the first sentence. The verdict scale drifts, and some copy implies tracking that doesn't exist.

changes.change: Game loop: options spaced on a log scale that all sound plausible, with a run of four guesses at most. Show an end-of-run screen ('7 of 11; biggest miss 300× too high'). Store Today's result on the device so a revisit shows it. Use 'Nobody knows' only where it is the true answer.
changes.why: The distractors are jokes, so players win by picking the modest option. The run has no end, and replays inflate the tally.

changes.change: Hero: name the paradox and data centres, e.g. 'One AI question is tiny. All of them together use about as much electricity as France.' Move the prototype ribbon into a small pill for user tests.
changes.why: The headline lists nouns and promises a method but gives no stakes, and the ribbon takes the first line of every screen.

changes.change: Number formatting: avoid thousands separators in prose ('28 kWh'). Normalise accents in search. Add a print stylesheet that is light, with sources expanded.
changes.why: Outside English-speaking countries, '28,000 Wh' reads as 28 Wh. Search strips accented characters, and teachers need a handout.

conflicts: The first card. The climate activist wants a systemic card first (coal, France-sized total), because the personal 'it's tiny' frame lets companies off the hook. The AI engineer and industry comms lead call the repeated scary world total a guilt trip and want a denominator (1.5%) and the IEA scenario range. C16 serves both by adding share and range while keeping the total. Which card leads is a founder decision.

The world line on share text. The activist wants it on every share line. The growth marketer, game designer and brand copywriter want it once and card-specific, because repeating it makes it boilerplate.

The bottle-of-water verdict. The AI engineer names the NO as the reason he'd share. The fact-checker, teacher, HN reader and industry lead say NO is premature without the GPT-4 email figure. The change list sides with evidence (C06).
Drafts. The Loudoun retiree wants the neighbour drafts promoted and more visible. The teacher wants a 'Reviewed only' filter on by default. The SEO specialist wants drafts noindexed.

Range-bar scale. The dataviz scientist, journalist and teacher want linear axes; the template chose log so a 500 ml claim fits on the same axis as 10 to 50 ml. A linear axis from 0 to 500 ml still fits.

Rejected or corrected reviewer claims (checked against reviewed.py and drafts.json): (1) The SEO specialist said 485 vs 480.6 compares consumption with consumption. Wrong: Ember's figure is national demand, which includes losses, while the IEA figure is data-centre consumption. (2) The Loudoun retiree called it a blocker that the bills page says no household-bill figure exists while the drafts cite $13.60. That is only partly right: the journalist notes $13.60 is a Dominion base-rate case with nothing cited tying it to data centres, so the unknown is narrowed rather than contradicted. (3) The fact-checker said the kettle's start temperature isn't stated. It is (15 °C, in the ladder footnote at template line 201), but 'at the very least' is still wrong because 99 Wh is a floor only from 15 °C. (4) The flight CO2e point (grid analyst, fact-checker, HN reader) and the PJM '11.5× not 9×' ratio (grid analyst) are plausible but can't be confirmed from Hum's own quotes, so they are listed as check-first items, not accepted as fact. (5) The game designer's '30× wrong' and others' '10 to 100×' for the phone-charge error depend on the charger wattage assumed. The verified part is 1.8% of a charge, and 'seconds' is unsourced.
The prototype ribbon. The UX designer wants it shrunk for testing; the honesty-minded reviewers praise the candour. A small 'Prototype' pill keeps both.
